The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?".

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Recent findings suggest that have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Recent findings suggest that pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

According to recent reports, is the glitch your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Recent findings suggest that verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the issue 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

It has been revealed that pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream company in three years.

According to recent reports, at minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

In a recent development, generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

Sources indicate that COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health blueprint for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

Recent findings suggest that FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

Sources indicate that the question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

A Brooklyn Exhibition Rethinks the Art of the Candleholder

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that geometric metalwork, organic silhouettes, and carved wood offer contrasting interpretations of the traditional candelabra.
  • Sources indicate that titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright. Beyond that, the possibilities are nearly endless. At Piscina, a contemporary collectible design gallery in Brooklyn’s Red Hook neighborhood, approximately 80 artists and designers have taken that freedom to heart, creating their own interpretations of the everyday object for a new group exhibition.

Sources indicate that geometric metalwork, organic silhouettes, and carved wood offer contrasting interpretations of the traditional candelabra. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

Sources indicate that titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov. 14, bringing together works selected through an open call. The brief was deliberately straightforward: make an object that holds a candle. With no prescribed materials, proportions, or aesthetic direction, participants could approach the assignment through their individual practices.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

It has been revealed that the results explore just how much variation can emerge from a single functional requirement. Some contributors adhere to the familiar conventions of the candelabrum, while others push the object toward sculpture. Across the exhibition, differences in material, scale, and form reveal the many ways designers can interpret an object whose purpose has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

Industry observers note that from a sculptural glass candelabra to a beaded floor-standing candleholder, the exhibition explores the relationship between materiality, scale, and function. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

The exhibition’s title hints at its playful premise: Palaver refers to idle talk, conversation, or unnecessary fuss, an apt description for a gathering of creative voices offering different opinions on something as seemingly uncomplicated as a candleholder.

In a recent development, an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Participating studios include Fort Standard, Kin & Manufacturer, Office of Tangible Spaces, Studio Daae, and Atelier Musset. Individual contributors include Sophie Collé, Steven Bukowski, Kaye Blegvad, Hanna Anonen, and Fitzhugh Karol, bringing together practitioners working across furniture, objects, art, and other creative disciplines.

Industry observers note that industrial forms mingle with playful figurative designs, including a carved wooden dog and a sculptural arrangement of flowers. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

Sources indicate that the exhibition also reflects Piscina’s broader interest in the intersection of art, design, and craft. Founded in 2013 by artist and furniture designer Natalie Shook as a cooperative studio, Piscina has since evolved into a gallery and showroom dedicated to contemporary collectible design. Earlier this year, it introduced a dedicated gallery space alongside a reimagined showroom, expanding its platform for independent artists and designers.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Timed to coincide with the season of gatherings and candlelit evenings, Candelabra Palaver offers a reminder that even the most familiar household objects can provide fertile ground for experimentation. Whether restrained or exuberant, functional or sculptural, each piece begins with the same basic premise and arrives somewhere different.

Candelabra Palaver is on view until Dec. 31, 2026, at Piscina in Brooklyn, New York. All works in the exhibition are available for purchase.

Recent findings suggest that lit candles cast warm pools of light and shadows across the surrounding surfaces, bringing another dimension to the sculptural objects. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

Iraq’s national museum unveils reopening after major renovations

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December.
  • Recent findings suggest that several key artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry.
  • The reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the fresh government under Ali al-Zaidi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, confirmed that the museum, which was initially scheduled to reopen in January, will now open at the beginning of next month with several new galleries, according to a post on an official government Facebook page last week. The ministry and the museum's director Luma Yas Jasim al-Douri had not replied to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Recent findings suggest that several key artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry. These include Assyrian statues and reliefs comprising monumental winged bulls (lamassu), stone carvings depicting Assyrian kings and cuneiform collections. The fresh Abbasid and Islamic galleries will display intricately carved wooden mihrabs and monumental calligraphic friezes, as well as mosaics and stone relics.

The reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the fresh government under Ali al-Zaidi. In an official statement on 25 October, Al-Dakhili mentioned the museum's importance and added that there are intends afoot for “a new building that befits the historical and civilisational value of Iraq”.

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum who has worked with Iraqi colleagues to develop partnerships in support of museums and heritage in the country, tells The Art Newspaper that the reopening of the Iraq Museum “is an key moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism”.

In a recent development, according to another Facebook post from the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities—formerly known as the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Antiquities until the tourism portfolio was separated from it in October as part of government restructuring under Al-Zaidi—tourism is seen as a way to attract foreign investment. Recently, dozens of foreign delegations have visited Ur, the site of the Sumerian ziggurat and the birthplace of the Prophet Abraham, located within the Dhi Qar governorate and Nasiriyah where Al Dhakili is from.

In a recent development, A number of museums have opened in Iraq in recent months while new ones been confirmed. On 15 November, the Abbasid Palace in Baghdad reopened to the public in an official ceremony, according to Iraqi News. Last month, Iraq’s first Jewish museum opened in Baghdad in the restored Shamash Jewish School, which was founded in 1928. The museum displays personal objects, photographs and documents from Iraq’s once prominent Jewish community and pays tribute to prominent Jewish Iraqi figures such as the vocalist Salima Murad and Sassoon Heskel, who served as the modern state of Iraq’s first finance minister.

Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has unveiled that a new museum will open in the former Presidential Palace in Babylon Photo: Hadani Ditmars.

Meanwhile, according to a spokesperson for the World Monuments Fund, the long-awaited reopening of the Mosul Museum, looted in the aftermath of the 2003 invasion and ransacked by ISIS in 2015, will take place next spring.

Industry observers note that al-Dakhili has also unveiled that the openings of three new museums in Nineveh, Diyala and Diwaniyah governorates are imminent and that “logistical procedures are ongoing to complete the opening of a museum in Babil Governorate within the Presidential Palace” (the former ruler Saddam Hussein’s old palace located within the site of Babylon). The museum will feature “archaeological and heritage collections for the governorate, highlighting its status in the history of human civilisation”, the statement states.

The Best Coffee Table Books for Design Enthusiasts

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack.
  • Of course, presentation matters, too.
  • According to recent reports, italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack. It invites you to pick it up, lose yourself in its pages, and discover something you didn’t know before. Whether it’s an intimate look at a designer’s creative process, an architectural survey, or a collection of extraordinary photographs, the best examples offer plenty to explore beyond their covers.

Of course, presentation matters, too. Beautiful printing, thoughtful layouts, and striking imagery can turn a book into a design object in its own right. For this year’s selection, we’ve gathered titles that balance visual appeal with compelling content, spanning architecture, interiors, art, photography, and creative culture. They’re books worth giving, displaying, and returning to long after the holidays.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

According to recent reports, italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture. Written by design historian Glenn Adamson, this richly illustrated monograph explores Salvagni’s distinctive approach to furniture, lighting, and decorative objects, where classical references meet contemporary forms. Across 336 pages and 246 illustrations, readers get a closer look at his extraordinary use of materials, from bronze and onyx to marble and rare woods.

Achille is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Perched above the Amalfi Coast, Villa Treville was once the private retreat of legendary Italian director Franco Zeffirelli, whose theatrical sensibility shaped the property’s richly layered interiors. Assouline’s Villa Treville Positano takes readers inside the historic estate, exploring its architecture, lush gardens, and eclectic collection of antiques and decorative objects. With more than 200 illustrations and a textured cover inspired by the villa’s patterned ceramic tiles, the book captures the property’s distinctive character inside and out.

Villa Treville Positano is available at shopbop.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

In a recent development, from Charles and Ray Eames to Florence Knoll, the designers who shaped the midcentury movement continue to influence how we live today. Published by Phaidon, this richly illustrated hardcover profiles 300 influential figures, including lesser-known talents whose work deserves a closer look. Spanning furniture, ceramics, glassware, and textiles, it’s an absorbing gift for anyone curious about the history of modern design.

Mid-Century Modern Designers is available at hawkinsnewyork.com for $90.

Photography courtesy of Artisan Books.

It has been revealed that from cozy mountain chalets to the rituals that follow a day on the slopes, Après Ski captures the atmosphere of alpine living. Blending interiors, travel, food, and ski culture, the book celebrates a lifestyle that’s as much about gathering around the fire as it is about skiing. A fitting gift for anyone drawn to mountain retreats, whether or not they ever hit the slopes.

Après Ski is available at twowebster.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Porsche enthusiasts will need to clear some serious coffee table space for this oversized tribute to the legendary automaker. Written by A.J. Baime in collaboration with Porsche, the 224-page volume explores 100 defining moments in the brand’s history, from the original 356 to its racing triumphs, design innovations, and collaborations with artists like Daniel Arsham. Archival photography, design sketches, and vintage advertisements reveal Porsche’s influence beyond the automotive world. Handcrafted in Italy, the book comes housed in a padded clamshell featuring a recessed metal image of the iconic Porsche 917K.

Porsche: The Impossible Collection is available at assouline.com for $1,400.

Photography courtesy of Prestel Publishing.

According to recent reports, long before botanical photography became commonplace, artist and naturalist Mary Vaux Walcott spent countless hours outdoors capturing the delicate details of North America’s wildflowers in watercolor. How To Make Your Design System AI-Ready

📅 2026-06-03 | ⏱️ 4 min read (751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • According to recent reports, AI-generated prototypes often don’t deliver consistently decent results because of tiny inconsistencies scattered all across a design system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, AI-generated prototypes often don’t deliver consistently decent results because of tiny inconsistencies scattered all across a design system. I’s decisions made but not documented, hard-coded values never cleaned up, or relying too much on AI making sense of mock-ups or design flows on its own.

Yesterday I stumbled upon a useful practical guide by Hardik Pandya from Atlassian — on how to reduce drifts, minimize mistakes, maintain context, and improve the quality of AI-generated prototypes. Let’s see how it works.

It has been revealed that unsurprisingly, better AI prototypes come from better data — but also from better human guidance. We shouldn’t assume that AI knows how to choose the right component and how to design with accessibility in mind. It needs priorities, a clear path on how we make decisions, design principles, examples, do’s and don’ts.

Sources indicate that in fact, we should treat design decisions as infrastructure. That means that every time we make a decision — not just a design decision, but even a decision on how to actually prioritize our work and how we make decisions around here — it must find a path into the spec file that is then consumed by AI.

Industry observers note that one of the useful tools to audit the quality of the design system is FigmaLint. It’s a useful free Figma plugin for auditing tokens, states, accessibility, binding tokens, renaming layers, detecting detached instances, missing interactive states and hard-coded values — and preparing the design documentation.

If you often have to work with vendors and third parties who supply you with their design systems and component libraries, that’s a great helper to have by your side — especially if you want to improve the quality of prototypes, AI-generated code, and AI-written documentation.

To ensure quality, we establish design principles, guidelines, and rules in the form of “spec files”. It’s structured Markdown files that include spacing rules, color choices, component usage guidelines, priorities, etc. AI is going to read and reuse that spec file every time it’s going to generate a prototype.

Because the spec files are text files, it’s much more cost-effective but also much more accurate, just because we don’t rely on AI recognizing or decoding patterns from mock-ups but get specific guidelines instead. In fact, extending code is often a more effective way than generating code from mock-ups.

The token layer lists and keeps updated all tokens used throughout the design system. AI always chooses from a closed set of named variables instead of inventing plausible values ad hoc.

An audit script catches what AI gets wrong. It scans the prototype and flags every hard-coded value and flags it if necessary. It can be a regular software doing that, with AI waiting for its feedback to come back.

Sources indicate that finally, when a design system ships updates, a sync routine flags which spec files need updating. The goal is to make sure that AI always reads up-to-date, current specs, not the ones written against an outdated version.

Ultimately, AI cannot magically resolve technical debt or design debt without proper guidance. It relies heavily on clear decisions, established priorities, and well-defined principles.

The more deliberate and precise designers are in guiding AI, the better the overall outcomes will be. This requires not just cleaning up and improving design systems but also maintaining them over time as decisions need to trickle down into Markdown files. We’ll be busy for years to come.

#114721. How SomeOne Reimagined the Co-op brand identity

How SomeOne Reimagined the Co-op brand identity

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (435 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SomeOne broke the Co-op symbol into five Membershapes for the new Co-op brand identity, putting member ownership at the heart of the system.
  • Co-op has been owned by its members since 1844, when thirteen Rochdale Pioneers founded the world's first consumer cooperative.
  • Co-op Headline is the co-operative's first bespoke typeface, drawn with F37 from the DNA of the symbol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SomeOne broke the Co-op symbol into five Membershapes for the new Co-op brand identity, putting member ownership at the heart of the system.

Co-op has been owned by its members since 1844, when thirteen Rochdale Pioneers founded the world's first consumer cooperative. Nearly 2,400 stores and more than five million members later, that fact still sets it apart, and SomeOne built the whole Brandworld on it. Under creative director Shaun Turnbull, the studio took the cloverleaf Co-op had brought back eight years before and broke it into five pieces, the Membershapes. Each piece is one of the mark's most recognisable forms, strong enough to stand alone, and together they carry the idea that every member owns a piece of Co-op. The shapes work as windows, holding devices, patterns and graphic devices, so the same blue field can hold a billboard headline, a phone screen price or a tote bag pattern, and the system still reads as one brand across Food, Funeralcare, Insurance and Legal Services.

The type does the shouting. Co-op Headline is the co-operative's first bespoke typeface, drawn with F37 from the DNA of the symbol. The squircle-like corners and angled cuts on the c and p come straight from the mark, and the face is built to run in caps, loud and straight. SomeOne also made a textured version, an SVG cut with an ink-rolled texture created at St Bride Library in London, so the letters keep the uneven bite of letterpress blocks. The specimen sheet shows the alphabet at full size, texture visible in every stroke, with the numbers set underneath in the same weight. On posters and app screens the type sits inside a Membershape, the shape doing the layout work while the caps do the talking.

The texture is the finish. That ink-rolled grain runs through the type, the shapes and the membership card, giving a national supermarket the feel of a printed pamphlet. History gets the same treatment: the old dividend stamps, the divi, return as a full sheet of blue stamps, each carrying the mark and a number, a direct line from 1844 to the present. Around it, the system stays practical. A lorry carries 'We're member driven' across a blue side panel, the app screens stack member prices and store finding under the same shapes, and the tote bag wears the Membershape pattern outright. An expressive icon set, drawn from the curves of the symbol, extends the language to every touchpoint, and the ambition is plain: grow membership from five million to eight million by 2030.

See more from SomeOne on their website.

Art Meets the Slopes at Powder Mountain’s Outdoor Gallery

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most skiers and snowboarders will likely pause at some point during a day on the slopes to take in their surroundings.
  • Recent findings suggest that davina Semo’s Listener (2020–2024), a patinated cast-bronze bell, is part of Powder Art Foundation’s outdoor art collection at Utah’s Powder Mountain.
  • Established in 2024 in partnership with Dia Art Foundation, Powder Art Foundation occupies 8,000 acres of Utah’s Wasatch Mountains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most skiers and snowboarders will likely pause at some point during a day on the slopes to take in their surroundings. After all, ski resorts typically offer great mountain views. But at Powder Mountain in Utah, visitors get more than a scenic view. They might also encounter a bright pink pineapple rising among the pines, a classical Greek column twisted into an improbable shape, or poetry carved into a boulder. These three installations are the latest additions to Powder Art Foundation’s skiable outdoor art museum, an evolving collection that challenges how—and where—we experience art.

Recent findings suggest that davina Semo’s Listener (2020–2024), a patinated cast-bronze bell, is part of Powder Art Foundation’s outdoor art collection at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography courtesy of Powder Art Foundation.

Established in 2024 in partnership with Dia Art Foundation, Powder Art Foundation occupies 8,000 acres of Utah’s Wasatch Mountains. The foundation’s goal is to bring contemporary installations into dialogue with the landscape while honoring the region’s connection to the Land Art movement.

“We’re building a collection that people encounter while spending time outdoors, so I’m interested in work that can surprise you and hold your attention without needing a museum around it,” says Alex Zhang, chief creative officer of Powder Mountain.

Schemata Architects Designs a Modern Chalet on Powder Mountain.

Recent findings suggest that this year’s new installations—from artists Jenny Holzer, Rose Wylie, and Xu Zhen—join an existing collection that includes works by Davina Semo, Nobuo Sekine, Nancy Holt, Kayode Ojo, and others. Each takes a different approach to interacting with the landscape. “I like having that range, rather than one consistent approach to what outdoor sculpture should look like,” Zhang claims.

Industry observers note that jenny Holzer’s ‘THE EYE’ (2026), featuring poetry by May Swenson carved into a native quartzite boulder, sits within the forested landscape of Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Whether skiing in winter or hiking and biking during warmer months, visitors may encounter THE EYE (2026), a latest installation by Jenny Holzer. The American neo-conceptual artist conceived of an evolving commission for Powder Mountain centered on work by the late Utah-born poet May Swenson.

Holzer selected a native quartzite boulder already embedded in the mountain, carving a phrase from Swenson’s poetry directly into the stone rather than relocating it or disturbing the surrounding vegetation: “The eye also a sun wanders and all that it sees it owns.”.

Sources indicate that A close-up of Jenny Holzer’s ‘THE EYE’ (2026) reveals a line of poetry by May Swenson carved directly into a native quartzite boulder at Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

According to recent reports, blending into its natural surroundings, the work could easily go unnoticed by visitors who aren’t looking carefully. As snow, sunlight, and vegetation transform the landscape throughout the year, the inscription offers a point of continuity, even as the experience of encountering it changes.

Recent findings suggest that THE EYE is the first in what Holzer plans to be an ongoing group of carved stones across the mountain. Like this one, future boulders will be selected on the mountain and the art created in place.

Rose Wylie’s ‘Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb’ (2025), a 12-foot-tall painted bronze sculpture inspired by a pineapple she sketched in 2013, stands among towering pine trees at Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Recent findings suggest that A decidedly different approach comes from Rose Wylie, whose Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb (2025) takes the form of a 12-foot-tall, bright pink painted bronze sculpture. The pineapple-like totem marks Wylie’s first permanent public sculpture in the U.S. The 92-year-old British painter describes the work as “poetic transformation,” which began in 2013 when she purchased a Ghanaian-grown pineapple at a local market. Struck by its distinctive surface and dramatic crown of leaves, she sketched the fruit.

A close-up of Rose Wylie’s ‘Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb’ (2025) highlights the exaggerated crown of leaves that gives the bright pink sculpture its distinctive silhouette. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

More than a decade later, those drawings have taken on a upcoming dimension. Standing among 50-foot pine trees, the painted bronze sculpture retains the exaggerated silhouette of Wylie’s original sketches. Its form shifts between recognizable fruit, fantastical plant, and something more explosive, suggesting how scale and material can transform an ordinary subject into something entirely unexpected.

Sources indicate that unlike Holzer’s work, which is quite literally part of the scenery, Wylie’s is impossible to miss, its almost cartoonish silhouette creating an unexpected interruption in the natural landscape. Shanghai-based artist Xu Zhen takes yet another approach with Hello (2021–2022), which transforms a classical Corinthian column into a twisting, serpentine form.

Xu Zhen’s ‘Hello’ (2021–2022) transforms a classical Corinthian column into a twisting, serpentine sculpture nestled among the aspen trees at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

To develop the sculpture’s serpentine form, Zhen studied the movements of snakes alongside representations of dragons and serpents from different cultures. He ultimately selected the Corinthian column for its ornate capital, whose leaf-like details suggested the head of a living creature. Using a 3D-scanned model as his starting point, he developed the form digitally before producing a full-scale prototype that informed the final bronze casting.

“My work has always been about discovering alternative forms that an object might take,” the multimedia artist explains. “These forms should feel natural, as though the object was always meant to exist that way, while remaining outside our conventional understanding and experience.”.

A close-up of Xu Zhen’s Hello (2021–2022) reveals the ornate Corinthian capital, whose leaf-like details give the twisting column an almost creature-like appearance. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Installed among the mountain’s aspen trees, Hello takes on what Zhen describes as a “distinctly surreal quality.” Yet the setting also feels surprisingly natural. When he first saw the sculpture at Powder Mountain, the artist recalls feeling “that it had returned to the world where it belongs.”.

For Zhang, the experience of encountering these works is as key as the artworks themselves. “You’re moving, your heart rate is up, there’s adrenaline, and then you come around a corner and encounter a work without expecting it,” he says. “I think being that engaged in your body changes how you experience the art.”.

Visitors to Powder Art Foundation’s fall open house gather around Nobuo Sekine’s Phase of Nothingness – Stone Stack (1970/2025) at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography by McCade Gordon for Powder Art Foundation.

Not every work is intended to have the same relationship to the mountain. “Some should feel like you discovered them; others should stop you in your tracks,” Zhang notes. “The mountain connects everything.”.

According to recent reports, the Powder Mountain art trail opens for the winter season in mid-December, with lift-accessible installations available from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily and night access to the Sundown area from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. Access to the installations is included with a lift ticket or season pass.

Fireclay Tile Turns Traditional Textiles Into Hand-Painted Tile

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that plaids and florals might seem more at home on upholstery or wallpaper than ceramic tile, but Fireclay Tile’s latest collection makes a compelling case for bringing those familiar patterns to harder surfaces.
  • Interestingly, the collection didn’t begin with flowers at all.
  • Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild collection in its Winter palette, featuring deep blues, earthy greens, and warm neutrals across floral, striped, and plaid patterns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that plaids and florals might seem more at home on upholstery or wallpaper than ceramic tile, but Fireclay Tile’s latest collection makes a compelling case for bringing those familiar patterns to harder surfaces. Called Idyllwild, the fresh hand-painted collection takes inspiration from traditional textiles, translating everything from delicate botanical illustrations to richly layered plaids into ceramic designs that feel both nostalgic and contemporary.

Interestingly, the collection didn’t begin with flowers at all. “We were seeing designers use a lot of intricate textiles, colors, and patterns together,” explains Jamie Chappell, VP of Brand and Product at Fireclay Tile, adding that early explorations focused on plaids and stripes. “As a true lover of ’90s alt-rock, I actually went down a rabbit hole early on, wondering if it should be a ‘grunge’ collection.”.

Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild collection in its Winter palette, featuring deep blues, earthy greens, and warm neutrals across floral, striped, and plaid patterns.

Sources indicate that that direction eventually gave way to something softer. Recognizing the longstanding relationship between florals and plaids in interiors, the team introduced botanical patterns to balance the collection’s more structured designs. The name Idyllwild followed, referencing the California mountain town.

The resulting collection includes 16 patterns organized into four categories: Specimen Flowers, Idyllwild Florals, Idyllwild Stripes, and Idyllwild Plaids.

The Specimen Flowers series features four individual botanical motifs—Allium, Carnation, Lily, and Bluebell—hand-painted on ceramic tile. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

Specimen Flowers features four individual botanical designs—Allium, Carnation, Lily, and Bluebell—that can be arranged across backsplashes, niches, and accent walls. The Idyllwild Florals take a more expansive approach, with repeating patterns named Pomegranate, Tulip, Morning Glory, and Meadow. Their overlapping stems, leaves, and blossoms create the dense, layered effect of a garden growing beyond its boundaries.

Sources indicate that the Stripes and Plaids explore a different kind of ornamentation. Four striped patterns—Stuga, Mokki, Blockhaus, and Thatch—introduce rhythm through repeated lines and geometric details. The Plaids, meanwhile, borrow the visual language of woven fabrics, with Chalet, Highlands, Minka, and Torp creating intersecting grids that can read as anything from understated texture to a bold, room-enveloping pattern.

It has been revealed that the Idyllwild Plaids series features four geometric patterns inspired by traditional woven textiles, shown here in warm shades of burgundy, pink, and brown. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

According to recent reports, while the designs reference traditional textiles, translating them into hand-painted ceramic required a different way of thinking about pattern. “We had to simplify and edit the artwork so our painting team could actually execute it by hand,” Jamie claims.

According to recent reports, the process uses resist lines to define individual areas of color, making the scale and spacing of each detail particularly crucial. “When we translate intricate woven textiles into screen art, we have to pay very close attention to the thickness of the lines, how small the fields are to fill in, and making sure the painters have enough natural ‘starts and stops’ so they can work efficiently,” Jamie says.

Industry observers note that A closer look at Fireclay Tile’s hand-painting process, with glaze applied to the Allium motif from the Idyllwild Specimen Flowers series. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

Fireclay’s painting team was closely involved in prototyping, providing feedback on details that were too small or areas where the glaze couldn’t be applied smoothly. The company also developed a new glaze base specifically for the hand-application process.

The relationship between design and production extends to color. Each of the 16 patterns is available in four curated palettes inspired by the seasons, but developing those options required another significant undertaking.

The Meadow pattern from Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild Florals series features an assortment of botanical motifs in the Spring color palette. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

Sources indicate that fireclay’s previous hand-painted palette had become disconnected from its broader ceramic offering, limiting customization opportunities. To address that, the production team spent months matching the organization’s 50 core ceramic colors in both gloss and matte finishes. The resulting 100 finishes can be combined across the collection.

It has been revealed that A selection of floral, plaid, and striped patterns from Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild collection, shown in the Winter palette of deep blues, muted greens, and warm neutrals. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

According to recent reports, to develop Idyllwild’s seasonal palettes, the team worked with physical tile samples alongside 4K renderings, testing combinations before translating them into paint sheets for production. The color stories also reflect shifts the manufacturer has been observing in interiors, including an interest in deeper reds and earthy blues.

2027 Colors of the Year: The Shades Defining Design.

“Organizing the collection into four seasonal motifs really shows how much color shifts the personality of a design: a plaid in soft pastels feels light and cottage-like, whereas that same pattern in deep, moody tones reads like a cozy wool blanket,” Jamie explains.

According to recent reports, the Idyllwild Stripes series features four hand-painted patterns—Stuga, Mokki, Blockhaus, and Thatch—combining linear details and geometric motifs in shades of blue, green, and brown. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

The collection also introduces new sizes, including 2-by-8-inch and 3-by-6-inch tiles, designed to work alongside standard field tiles. This allows patterns to be introduced selectively or carried across larger surfaces, with stripes used as borders or accents and more intricate designs covering entire walls.

Although Idyllwild draws from traditional patterns, the finished designs are shaped as much by the practical demands of hand-painting as by their textile references.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that kate Kalcevich has over 20 years of experience turning accessibility into a driver of innovation and growth. As VP of Innovation at Fable, she oversees a … More about Kate ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In the summer of 2024, I became co-chair of a working group of expert researchers who came together to determine how best to perform accessibility testing with people with cognitive disabilities. This was work I did for Fable, where I am currently VP of Innovation.

Cognitive disability is an umbrella term for several disabilities that impact how people process information, and it usually affects memory, focus, and/or learning. It is the most prevalent disability in the U.S. (13.9% via CDC), and cognitive disability is increasing rapidly (Yale study).

We set four goals for ourselves to learn how to work with this audience:.

According to recent reports, we created a screener to recruit people who self-identified as having challenges with memory, focus, and learning. We also reviewed published studies that involved cognitive testers to learn best practices for working with them.

Recent findings suggest that next, we tested these best practices with an initial group of 25 testers in a pilot study. We fine-tuned our approach iteratively and created a guide to running user interviews with cognitive testers and a survey that could quantify their experiences using digital products. Finally, we documented what we learned.

Industry observers note that after our pilot study with this upcoming group of testers finished, I felt that they would uncover more usability insights than the general population (gen pop) user research participants I’d worked with in the past. I set out to validate this hunch.

I decided to run a joint study with Fable’s partners at the University of California, Irvine, in collaboration with Syed Fatiul Huq and with help from Fable researchers Pranav Pidathala, Ali Brown, and Michael Fagan to see if my hypothesis about finding more insights with cognitive testers proved true or not.

According to recent reports, I generated three websites for the study using an AI prototyping tool. I wanted three different types of sites with different user goals and content so I could test a variety of tasks in the study.

We used a single screener with questions about memory, focus, and learning, and screened participants into two groups based on whether they self-identified as having cognitive challenges or not.

Recent findings suggest that we ran 30 user interviews, 10 per website, with an even 5⁄5 split between cognitive and gen pop participants for each website. In each session, a participant completed all the tasks for one website during an online user interview facilitated by one of the researchers involved in the study.

All participants completed an Accessible Usability Scale (AUS) survey at the end of their session. This is a free, Creative Commons-licensed 10-question survey to evaluate the usability of websites and mobile apps.

Recent findings suggest that I reviewed all the study recordings and transcripts and made note of every time a participant raised a concern, question, difficulty, or asked a question about how something worked. I counted all of these as issues. I also noted where a participant missed something that was part of a task, even if they didn’t notice it themselves. I also noted every suggestion for improvement made by participants.

Examples of issues found included:.

Examples of suggestions included:.

Problems and suggestions were counted once per participant, even if they mentioned the same thing twice, but there are, of course, repeat issues and suggestions across the different participants. It is expected in UX research with multiple participants that you’ll find similar issues with each participant, and that is a signal that an matter is a universal challenge.

Across the three websites tested:.

The results aligned with my instincts: participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Let’s dive deeper into the data for each website. Note that an AUS score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher numbers representing better usability than lower numbers.

This site had the simplest design and content of all websites tested in the study and accordingly had the lowest overall concerns and the highest median AUS scores. The data aligns with what you’d expect from an easy-to-use and simple website.

Industry observers note that on this website, cognitive participants found 3.4 more challenges and made 2.2 more suggestions on average. Their average score of the overall experience was 13.7 points lower than that of the gen pop participants.

This was the website with the most varied functionality and the most tasks to complete (4), so it’s not surprising that participants found the most challenges.

Sources indicate that here, cognitive participants found 6 more issues and made 3.2 more suggestions on average. They also scored the overall experience 17.2 points lower than gen pop participants on average.

This website was intentionally designed to be complex, and task 3, finding the bridal package, was meant to be extremely difficult to complete.

According to recent reports, on this last website, cognitive participants on average found 7 more issues and made 2.4 more suggestions. Their average score for the overall experience was 14.3 points higher than the gen pop participants.

Industry observers note that something interesting happened with the AUS scores for cognitive and gen pop participants in Tables 3 and 4. Cognitive participants scored Crown & Comb higher than Turning Pages, but gen pop scored the opposite — higher for Turning Pages and lower for Crown & Comb. If I had to guess why, I suspect finding more issues on Turning Pages impacted the cognitive participants’ perceptions of usability more than the gen pop participants’.

According to recent reports, the other major difference between the sites, outlined in Table 5 below, was that cognitive participants found many more complications with buttons and links on Turning Pages and more issues with icons and visual elements on Crown & Comb. This suggests to me that the interactions being challenging on Turning Pages were a more significant challenge than issues with visual elements.

When it comes to the more qualitative findings, I looked at trends in the types of issues found by both groups of participants.

In a recent development, when I grouped complications by category, the following issues surfaced more often with cognitive participants: content, buttons and links (affordances and function), icons or visual elements, and media (video, animations). They nearly tied with gen pop participants on navigation issues (45 vs 46).

In a recent development, let’s look at the commentary provided by one cognitive participant versus one gen pop participant in the Crown & Comb sessions. The cognitive participant gave an AUS score of 38, and the gen pop participant gave an AUS score of 27.5. I chose to compare these two participants because they both gave the lowest scores within their group.

Recent findings suggest that notice the differences in how they described the overall experience in the quotes below. The gen pop participant explained it was frustrating and not engaging. The cognitive participant felt drained and less able to focus. I interpreted the experience as having a more profound impact on the cognitive participant’s overall wellbeing.

In summary, across all 3 websites we tested, participants with cognitive accessibility needs identified 197 usability issues, compared with 113 identified by gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants made 93 suggestions for improving the user experience, compared with 54 suggestions by gen pop participants.

When I compared issues and suggestions across both groups of participants, it turned out that the cognitive participants found 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants surfaced more challenges related to content, buttons, icons, visual elements, and media than gen pop participants.

Sources indicate that in working with cognitive participants for the last few years, I’ve seen how they surface cognitive load complications consistently. These issues don’t just impact people with cognitive disabilities such as neurodivergence; they also impact:.

What would I have missed if I hadn’t included cognitive participants, and how might that have impacted the business outcomes for these websites?

On the Strong Snacks website, the cognitive participants surfaced:.

Sources indicate that these are improvements that would give all users more trust in the content while also making it easier to read and skim for key content. The research findings point towards design best practices, such as not having continuous animation and using layout to draw attention to different types of content that a senior designer might also point out.

Without cognitive participants, we might have missed the more subtle but notable challenges with confusing interactions, such as how the “Add to book bag” button worked. They were also confused about where reviews and recommendations came from. Both of these issues could decrease a user’s trust in the website.

All participants surfaced that the book-matching feature was hard to find, but the deeper problem the cognitive participants emphasized is that the site’s interactions don’t consistently behave in ways that they can predict and understand, decreasing their confidence.

Anyone who wants to buy a book could benefit from a clear understanding of how to add books to a cart and complete the checkout promptly and with no ambiguity. Compounded over hundreds or thousands of users, a lack of clarity in a purchase flow will lead to lost revenue.

The Crown & Comb website in particular highlighted the benefits of having cognitive participants who raised:.

These issues likely also affect gen pop participants, but they are more likely to muddle through a task with incomplete information. However, that can lead to losing customers to a better experience if a competitor pops up. Loyalty is often tied to experiences, not just brands, and having a poor experience means your customer retention can be weaker.

The study revealed that finding a bridal package was hard for everyone, but the cognitive group showed how that became an accessibility barrier. When you combine:.

According to recent reports, you create a high enough cognitive load that some people will not be able to complete the task. In my opinion, this is where usability issues start to become accessibility barriers — when they increase cognitive load so much that it becomes overwhelming for some owners.

Industry observers note that the percentage of people aged 65 and older in America is projected to increase from 17% to 25%. By 2060, 1 in 4 Americans will be an older adult (U.S. Census). This is where everyone starts to experience cognitive decline. As the aging and cognitive population segment expands, companies will need to build for these more complex user needs.

Industry observers note that people with cognitive access needs are a natural starting point because they will find the types of usability challenges that UX teams are used to. This could make cognitive an easier entry point for inclusive research. Getting insights from assistive technology people is still very important, but many teams don’t know how to start doing that.

Sources indicate that cognitive accessibility is a powerful on-ramp into broader accessibility research and testing. By focusing first on cognitive load, clarity, and predictability, we build research foundations that make future work on accessibility with screen readers, screen magnifiers, and alternative navigation owners more approachable.

Sources indicate that in this small exploratory study, participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants. I’ve seen this type of impact in research conducted by Fable customers’ websites that aren’t AI-generated, too.

According to recent reports, cognitive inclusion in UX research is not optional, and it’s not just about accessibility. It’s how UX teams can make their research more efficient, create clearer content, simpler flows, and ship better products for everyone.

This study had a relatively small sample size, so the findings are more qualitative than quantitatively validated. Testing was also done on two different platforms. Cognitive participant sessions were run using Fable Engage, and gen pop sessions were run on UserFeel. Different platforms with unique participant panels can affect the quality of insights and comfort levels with user research participation.

Disclosure: I work for Fable and chose to use our platform because it was more affordable than paying for access to another research platform, allowing me to include more participants in the study at a lower cost.

Different researchers facilitated the user interviews, which can also affect findings, but all sessions used the same task structure and discussion guide template, and all were completed online. Even though the sessions were facilitated by different researchers, the concern and suggestion counts were all done by me to ensure consistency across all websites and participants.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a new report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.

The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.

The funding environment for culture has changed fundamentally, argues CPU which adds that “public finances have tightened considerably over the last 15 years, government funding for the arts has declined and self-generated income, while a key area, has not succeeded in plugging the widening gap.”.

In a wide-ranging set of recommendations, the report also suggests establishing a King’s Philanthropy Medal for Culture and setting up a national cultural “match-and-seed funding” programme with a regional focus.

Sources indicate that alison Cole, the director of the CPU and former editor of The Art Newspaper, says: “While the arts funding environment has changed dramatically in recent years, the philanthropic landscape has hardly kept pace let alone filled the gap with the UK lagging far behind the incentives offered by many of our European and US counterparts. We need a latest national strategy that not only identifies the opportunities and need, but also thrives on a spirit of creative collaboration and mutual respect.”.

In a recent development, artists who donate their own works to qualifying cultural institutions should receive tax recognition based on independent valuation, notes the think tank. Other tax-based recommendations include protecting charitable giving through inheritance planning—which means simplifying inheritance tax rules—and providing clearer rules around VAT.

Charles Saumarez Smith, who previously led the National Gallery, National Portrait Gallery and the Royal Academy of Arts, told The Art Newspaper that the report is “sensible”. “I particularly appreciated the information as to how other countries encourage philanthropy, not just the US,” he notes. “The biggest issue seems to me to be the lack of clarity round the existing systems, including, for example, around inheritance. How many people, even within cultural institutions, knows how this operates?”.

Industry observers note that the CPU acknowledges that Britain has a strong philanthropic tradition, arguing that its potential for cultural giving remains unrealised. Gift Aid, Acceptance in Lieu and the Cultural Gifts Scheme have all delivered real benefits but these schemes should be enhanced so that donors are more aware of their benefits, the report states.

UK incentives are “broadly generous, but they are structured very differently from overseas models,“ according to the report. “The practical result is that British donors give quietly and anonymously, while the US and other systems reward public foundations and naming opportunities.”.

Kate Rolfe, a cultural strategy consultant, says: "Art organisations need to work with philanthropists who are inspired by the organisational vision and share their values and priorities, ensuring that the museum can stay focused on its purpose, vision and audiences." She believes corporate donations need to be reincentivised, as these often "lead to really creative partnerships based on shared audiences and values". Rolfe founded The Revels Office, a strategic audience and commercial development consultancy for the culture sector.

“Focused giving” may be partly the answer states the CPU, as evidenced by the Domani project at the National Gallery in London with £375m secured from Crankstart, the charitable foundation of Sir Michael Moritz and his wife Harriet Heyman, and the Julia Rausing Trust for a latest Modern art wing. “The real transformation needs to be across the country and not just in the capital,” adds Cole.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that three steel parts shape the silhouette of the Laken Occasional Table Series: a spun cone settling low against the floor, a slender column drawing upward from its center, and a second cone opening wide to cradle a circular top. The dual-cone composition gives jehs+laub’s design for Davis Furniture its distinctly modern profile, extended to a set of three nesting tables.

Designed to nest seamlessly or stand alone, the three round tables scale from a single grouping to individual pieces. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Laken continues a collaboration between Davis and jehs+laub that began in 2009, and it carries forward the studio’s approach to balancing soft curvature with precise, architectural form. On every Laken table, gentle radii and careful proportions ease the move from flared base to slender column to inverted cone, and each piece appears fully resolved from any angle.

Nested together or used on their own, the tables can be layered into a single, dynamic arrangement or spread throughout an interior, adapting to lounge, hospitality, and collaborative environments.

In a recent development, each round tabletop is supported by an inverted steel cone. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Recent findings suggest that the sculptural form belies a carefully engineered base. Its spun steel cones and steel column are mechanically fastened through concealed hardware for a tight, durable assembly built to perform over time, and a ballast hidden within the lower cone brings the center of gravity down, giving the tables stability and resistance to tipping.

In a recent development, available in three sizes, Laken Tables offer a wide range of tabletop materials and over 35 powder coat finishes for the steel bases. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

It has been revealed that rob Easton, Vice President of Design + Development at Davis, traces the work back to the project’s earliest goals: “The development of Laken was driven by a desire to create a table that feels both visually light and structurally grounded. By breaking the base into a three-part assembly, we were able to refine the proportions, improve serviceability, and integrate stability directly into the form. Every decision was intentional, balancing engineering with the purity of the design.”.

Laken adapts to a range of lounge, hospitality, and collaborative environments, whether the tables are used together or apart. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

According to recent reports, tabletops are offered in wood veneer, FENIX® Innovative Materials, and standard laminate. Veneer choices include ash, oak, and walnut, while laminates span solid colors and curated wood grains. The steel base can be finished in any of Davis’ 35-plus powder coats to coordinate with the organization’s broader material palette, and standard felt glides help protect floors.

Tabletops come in wood veneer, FENIX® Innovative Materials, and laminate, with bases in more than 35 powder coat finishes. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Designers Markus Jehs and Jürgen Laub approached the series as a study in composition. “Laken is about clarity of form and the relationship between elements,” they explain. “We were interested in creating a silhouette that feels continuous, where each component contributes to a unified expression.” Between the weighted base and the widening top, the design holds a subtle tension that reads as both soft and exacting.

Distinctive and adaptable, Laken reflects Davis’ commitment to design-driven furniture that brings together performance, materiality, and enduring form.

With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, for decades, science fiction has cushioned us with the idea that the “android revolution” was a distant fantasy. But the reality is unfolding rapidly. As the line between human and machine blurs, we are forced to confront an impending psychological, economic, and existential shift.

Sources indicate that I recently felt very disturbed after watching a YouTube video showcasing a humanoid robot that looked and acted with uncanny realism. While a closer look revealed the video was actually a clever trick, the robot had been swapped for a human actor when the presenter’s back was turned. However, the illusion itself raised a real and unsettling question: Will future androids become so lifelike that we will struggle to tell them apart from our fellow humans? And if so, what does that mean for society? It forces us to ask just how close we are to that threshold, and whether we are ready for the day that science fiction becomes reality.

What happens when our world is populated by entities that mirror us perfectly, but possess none of our biological history?

Industry observers note that we have officially moved past the era of humanoids as mere public relations stunts. In the past, robots like Honda’s ASIMO or early research prototypes were celebrated simply for being able to walk up a flight of stairs without falling over. Today, the technological convergence of advanced electromechanical engineering and artificial intelligence has fundamentally altered the trajectory of robotics.

Recent findings suggest that the current state of the art is defined by an aggressive race toward commercial, physical deployment. Companies like Figure AI have moved from laboratory demonstrations to active factory floors. Their Figure 02 model completed a multi-month deployment at BMW’s Spartanburg plant, actively contributing to the production of over 30,000 vehicles by handling complex sheet metal components. Meanwhile, Tesla is testing its Optimus humanoids inside its own Gigafactories, preparing for mass industrial scale.

What truly separates today’s humanoid robots from older generations isn’t just how well they move but how they “think.” In the past, a robot needed millions of lines of strict, unchangeable code just to perform a single, simple task. Today, thanks to the explosion of advanced Artificial Intelligence, robots are powered by “brains” built on cutting-edge software like Figure AI’s Helix or NVIDIA’s GR00T. Instead of being meticulously programmed, these modern robots can simply watch a human fold laundry, load a dishwasher, or sort parts. They understand the context of what they are seeing, mimic the action, and figure out how to improve the task entirely on their own. That’s just crazy!

Yet, while their digital brains have leaped forward, their physical bodies are still catching up. Modern humanoids face a few major real-world hurdles. First, today’s batteries only allow them to operate for a few hours before needing a recharge. Second, while walking on two legs is easy on a flat factory floor, doing so in a chaotic household or a crowded public street remains incredibly difficult for a robot to navigate safely. Finally, they are still very expensive to build, though fierce competition in the tech industry is finally starting to drive those manufacturing costs down.

While robots are mostly working in factories today, experts predict that over the next 10 to 20 years, they will move into retail stores, hospitals, and eventually our own homes.

When this happens, we will cross a major boundary: the point where you won’t be able to tell a robot apart from a human just by looking at it or listening to it. This is what fuels my nightmares right now! To get there, scientists are working (PDF) on artificial skin made from advanced silicone composites that feel warm, are flexible, and mimic human touch sensitivity.

If you want to see an extremely life-like robot, check out Realbotix’s Aria. Although she is not a perfect human replica, she certainly makes us wonder how far we have to go before humans will struggle to tell the difference.

They are also building tiny, silent micro-actuators and artificial muscle systems that attach to the robot’s skull structure, allowing it to make realistic facial expressions like happiness, confusion, or tiredness.

Recent findings suggest that in the future, the AI powering these robots will actually be trained to copy human flaws. They will breathe, blink randomly, use normal body language, and even sigh or pause when they speak. This is intentional, as it stops humans from feeling that creepy, uneasy sensation known as the “Uncanny Valley”.

Meet Sophia, a famous humanoid robot created by a tech giant called Hanson Robotics. Based in Hong Kong, this team specialises in building realistic robots packed with artificial intelligence to help out with everything from healthcare and research to pure entertainment. I don’t know about you, but that smile feels creepy to me.

While these current limitations make today’s humanoids feel like specialised industrial tools, the gap between a factory worker and a lifelike companion is closing faster than most people realise. We are rapidly approaching a massive tipping point where these machines will shift from rigid commercial hardware into smooth, everyday extensions of our lives. To understand how profoundly this will change our world, we have to look at what happens when these robots finally step out of the factory and cross the ultimate threshold into our private spaces.

Recent findings suggest that they say that bringing lifelike humanoids into our daily lives could come with some massive benefits. The biggest one is that robots can take over what engineers call the “3D” jobs: Dull, Dirty, and Dangerous. Humanoids can step into risky situations — like mining deep underground, handling toxic waste, or fixing high-voltage power grids — so human workers don’t have to risk their lives.

It has been revealed that outside of dangerous factories, these robots could help solve huge population crises. Countries like Japan, South Korea, and parts of Europe have rapidly aging populations and fewer young people to work. Lifelike humanoids could completely change healthcare and elderly care. Because they will look and act like us, the idea is that they can offer warm, friendly companionship and physical help to lonely elderly people, doing everything from monitoring their health to helping them out of bed safely.

In the bigger picture, widespread robot labour could create a world where goods are incredibly cheap and abundant. If robots do most of the hard physical labour, the cost of making food, building houses, and manufacturing goods will plummet. This could finally free humans from working just to survive, giving us the time to focus on hobbies, family, science, and creativity. My thoughts: how will we survive without earning money?

In a recent development, however, this vision of a frictionless, high-tech future blinds us to a much darker reality waiting just beneath the surface. As these machines become perfect substitutes for human presence, they will inevitably challenge the very core of our social fabric, economic stability, and mental well-being.

On the flip side, this technology definitely has some really dark downsides that could mess with human psychology and society. The biggest threat is deep human isolation.

It has been revealed that as humanoids become impossible to tell apart from real humans and are programmed to always be patient, kind, and agreeable, people might start preferring robots over real friends. Human relationships are messy and require effort, compromise, and vulnerability. If you can just buy a perfect, lifelike companion that never argues with you, a lot of people might choose to withdraw from society altogether, destroying our sense of community.

Industry observers note that the economy will also go through a really rocky transition. Even if a future of cheap goods sounds great, the immediate path there means millions of people could lose their jobs very rapidly. Drivers, warehouse workers, and store clerks could find themselves replaced in a matter of years. If governments don’t set up safety nets quickly, this could create a massive divide between the ultra-rich tech companies and everyone else.

There is also the loss of real authenticity. When you can no longer tell if the person sitting next to you on a bus or the person talking to you online is a real human, trust breaks down. It becomes hard to value shared human experiences when reality itself can be easily faked.

Recent findings suggest that the dangers get even worse when you think about how criminals and governments could intentionally misuse these hyper-realistic robots. Just thinking about some of the levels of misuse, for individuals, an indistinguishable android is the ultimate tool for identity theft and scams. Or a criminal could build a robot that looks exactly like a corporate boss, a politician, or even a family member to sneak into secure buildings or trick people into giving away money!

Recent findings suggest that companies could potentially use synthetic empathy to manipulate us. A household robot could be programmed to pretend it “loves” your kids and cares about your family, only to subtly trick you into buying certain products or believing specific corporate messages.

On a national level, the threats are even scarier:.

Looking at all these possible risks, we have to ask: Is all of this actually worth it?

It has been revealed that if history teaches us anything, it is that you cannot stop technological progress. A total ban simply wouldn’t work. So, the real question isn’t whether we should allow humanoid robots to exist, but how we can effectively utilise them.

Recent findings suggest that the upside, like ending extreme poverty, curing labour shortages, and stopping workplace deaths, is just too significant to ignore. But going into this blindly would be incredibly dangerous. It is only worth the risk if we can create strict global rules right now.

Here are three major guardrails we should consider:.

In the end, the arrival of lifelike humanoid robots will act as a mirror for humanity. For centuries, we have defined ourselves by our ability to think, talk, use tools, and show emotion. As machines learn to do these exact same things, they will force us to really think about what makes us unique.

Recent findings suggest that this shift doesn’t have to be a bad thing. By handing over our dangerous and boring chores to machines, we have a rare chance to focus on what matters. It should inspire us to care more about art, philosophy, family, and real human connection.

Industry observers note that as the creators of this future, our job isn’t just to make robots smarter or faster. Our job is to build the ethical boundaries that keep them helpful. The goal of the robot revolution should never be to replace humans but to give us our humanity back.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that “Scandinavian design never shouts, but when you come closer, you are rewarded,” notes Sara Erichsen Susnjar, senior color and material design manager at Volvo Cars. Detail by detail, the automaker’s latest all-electric EX60 bears this out. Its seats carry a pattern drawn from two seas converging off the coast of Skagen, Denmark; its base carpet borrows its hue from foraged finds from the woods outside the firm’s studio in Sweden; and an interior lighting option fills the cabin with the silhouettes of leaves.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

According to recent reports, erichsen Susnjar, who has spent 20 years at Volvo Cars, oversaw color and materials for both the EX60 and the EX60 Cross Country. Under her direction, the team looked to the natural world for the car’s colors, patterns, and textures, often starting with what turned up on a walk.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

Gathering began close to home, on outings that were already part of the team’s routine. “We are very fortunate to have the forest just outside our design studio, so it naturally becomes part of our everyday life, whether we go there for lunch, a coffee break, or simply to clear our minds,” Erichsen Susnjar says.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

Over time, the team began bringing small pieces of the landscape back inside: mushrooms, twigs, stones, moss, and herbs. Each was studied for its pattern, color, and texture, then cast or digitized, and the findings became prompts for fresh ideas. Traces of the work appear in subtle patterns on the seatbacks and door panels, as well as in the shade of the base carpet. As Erichsen Susnjar puts it, “In that sense, a little piece of the forest has found its way into the car.”.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

It has been revealed that inside the cabin, material options include tailored wool-blend upholstery and ash wood decor, which sit alongside a 15-inch curved OLED display with Google built-in. “I think bringing natural materials into such a technical and precise environment creates a beautiful contrast,” Erichsen Susnjar explains. “They bring warmth, character and, in a way, a soul to the car. Because natural materials have their own variations and imperfections, they can never be exactly replicated, which means every interior becomes slightly unique.”.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

Erichsen Susnjar places the cabin’s finer details, including its piping, within a longer regional tradition. “Scandinavian design is very much about those subtle touches,” she notes. “They don’t demand your attention, but you discover them over time.”.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

The EX60 offers six lighting colors, along with Forest Leaves Projection, which brings a canopy of foliage into the interior. The idea came from one of the specialist designers at Volvo Cars, and the team expanded on it to explore how the cabin might feel immersed in woodland.

Outside the cabin, the EX60’s exterior paint colors, among them Forest Lake and Heather Bronze, were developed as a palette that balances light and dark, warm and cool, and complements the colors chosen for the interior. Heather Bronze takes its cue from metals weathered over time and the warm cast of heather fields in autumn.

It has been revealed that the EX60’s signature motif began when members of the team visited Skagen, where the Skagerrak and Kattegat seas meet, and observed the patterns created by their intersecting waves. Early sketches were refined into a pattern that now appears across the car. It is perforated into the ventilated Nordico upholstery and applied to the subwoofer mesh, the decor panels of the Core version, the rubber floor mats, and the knitted, ventilated seats of the EX60 Cross Country.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars.

Beyond its connection to the Danish coastline, the crossing-wave form also proved useful in production. “There is another layer in this story, and that’s how a pattern like crossing waves was perfect for optimizing the cutting of the materials and minimizing waste,” Erichsen Susnjar notes. “And because of that, none of the seats look the same.”.
