  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Industry observers note that the way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking. He has over 25 years experience working with clients such as Doctors … More about Paul ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that the way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy. If it were turned into a movie, reviewers would say it was unbelievable. Nobody could be that stupid.

Sources indicate that yet here we are. And what makes it all the more frustrating is that we have been here before.

In a recent development, back in 2014, I wrote a book for Smashing Magazine called Digital Adaptation, looking at the mistakes being made in how organizations were approaching digital transformation and what they should be doing instead. The similarities between then and now are striking.

So in this post, I want to look back at Digital Adaptation and see how the lessons in that book apply to the AI era and what we can learn from the past to help us navigate the challenges of AI today.

The biggest mistake, both then and now, is approaching each as a technological challenge.

According to recent reports, sure, both digital transformation and AI are technological advances, and yes, some level of technological implementation is required. But that is the tip of a very large iceberg.

Sources indicate that back in the midst of the digital transformation era, IT departments were rolling out CMSs, CRM systems, intranets, and so on. Meanwhile, on the customer-facing side, organizations were rolling out websites, apps, and personalization. But they were putting almost no emphasis on how people were going to use these systems.

Internal systems were hard to use, and customers either didn’t care what was being built or wanted something else entirely.

It has been revealed that the same is happening with AI. Senior management are buying into the hype, and IT teams are rolling out Copilot Studio licenses company-wide and considering the job done. Sure, there is a bit of organization-wide generic training, but that’s about it.

Just like before, staff are left wondering what to do with these latest systems and feeling under pressure to use them and deliver results.

According to recent reports, after all, this time around, it is even worse, because this time, staff fear for their jobs. They have read the same headlines that you have, and no amount of promises from senior management is going to make them feel any better.

I mean, think about it from a staff member’s point of view. AI offers them very little personally, even setting aside the fact that management may be intending to use it to replace them.

The main reason senior management are excited about AI is that it provides additional productivity. People can do more in less time. But that does not benefit staff. They are still required to work 9 to 5, but now they are expected to do more in the same time. They don’t get any time back, and they don’t get paid more, so why would they embrace AI?

One strategy is to help staff identify the parts of their job they hate and how AI can help them do those tasks more promptly and less painfully. People tend to be a lot more receptive to change when it is presented as an opportunity to improve their working lives.

According to recent reports, but, that should just be the beginning. Organizations may need to consider providing incentives for staff to adopt AI in terms of career progression, compensation, or shorter working hours.

Recent findings suggest that also, adopting AI is not a simple task. It involves challenging every working practice they have built up over (in some cases) decades. All of that procedural knowledge has to be rebuilt. That is a lot to ask of anybody in even the best of circumstances, and most employees do not find themselves in the best of circumstances.

Most are overworked and struggling to stay on top of their to-do lists. They don’t have time to sit down, learn a upcoming tool, and figure out how it fits into their workflow.

That doesn’t just take time. It also takes a lot of consideration and experimentation. It is not enough to just send a member of staff on a training course and expect them to be able to use AI to its full potential.

At a minimum, staff need training specific to their roles, such as the AI training I provide to UX teams. But organizations should be going even further.

In a recent development, they need to develop sophisticated training programs that help staff from different departments understand how to use AI in their specific roles. They need ongoing support and the time to experiment with AI to find the best ways to use it.

Recent findings suggest that but formal training will only take you so far. In my experience, the most effective support comes from colleagues, which is why I would start with the enthusiasts rather than the resisters. Every organization has a handful of people who are already experimenting with AI, often without anybody asking them to. Bring those people together, give them the time and space to share what is working for them, and let their enthusiasm spread to everyone else.

Sources indicate that I saw this work during the digital transformation era too. In Digital Adaptation, I described an internal conference where staff indicated their colleagues what they had built, and it did more for adoption than any memo from the top ever could. People are far more likely to try something when they see a colleague in a similar role using it successfully than when they are told to by senior management.

Unfortunately, experimentation comes with a major downside… mistakes will be made.

Sources indicate that many organizations have, to be frank, a culture of fear where mistakes are seen as a sign of incompetence. However, by its very nature, learning a fresh tool like AI will involve making mistakes, and this can be a massive barrier to adoption.

I saw this during the era of digital transformation. Senior management would demand digital transformation and were confused when it didn’t happen.

What they didn’t realize was that they were sending mixed messages to staff. Sure, they were asking for digital transformation, but they were still demanding that the same key performance indicators (KPIs) be met, and they still pointed out any mistakes in their annual reviews.

There was no space to fail, as the pressure to deliver was relentless.

Recent findings suggest that this time around, it seems to be even worse. I hear horror stories of staff being reprimanded for using too many tokens just weeks after being told to adopt AI. Or staff being lectured so much about what they should or should not do with AI that they are afraid to try anything. It is safer to just do what they have always done.

Look, I get it. AI cannot be rolled out without some governance in place, but again, this is an area that organizations have typically handled poorly.

In the midst of digital transformation, governance would either be non-existent, or it would be so strict that it would stifle innovation, and unfortunately, I see the same pattern emerging with AI adoption.

Industry observers note that staff need some governance to help them know where they stand. It helps them understand what is expected of them and what they can and cannot do.

But too often organizations have been so strict that it is easier not to do anything at all. Pages of instructions about what people should and should not share with AI create that sense of fear that I mentioned earlier.

Of course, mistakes will get made, but that is the cost of change, and so organizations need to accept that and do what they can to mitigate that in how they roll out the technology.

In a recent development, that said, organizations will need to be careful in how they roll out AI from an IT perspective. Once again, it is easy to lock everything down and stifle the adoption of AI.

Industry observers note that again, this is something I highlighted back in 2014 with digital transformation. Overstretched IT teams would pick a set of technologies and roll them out organization-wide, often with little or no consultation with the individuals who would be using them. Anything outside of that set of technologies had to go through a complex approval process, normally involving a steering committee. The result was a glacial pace of change that was one of the major contributing factors to the failure rate of digital transformation projects.

Sources indicate that today we are seeing the same thing. IT teams are opting into a tool like Copilot and calling it a day, but that often falls massively short.

Take, for example, a UX team I am working with at the moment. Management is pushing hard for AI adoption, and the team is excited about the potential of creating an AI-powered research repository and even AI personas. It sounds like a wonderful case study in AI adoption, with enthusiastic management, an excited team, and innovative ideas.

Unfortunately, the reality is that nothing is happening because Copilot cannot deliver on the team’s vision, and so they are presently bogged down in bureaucracy as they try to persuade the AI steering group that they need to use a different toolset. Understandably, the team’s enthusiasm is waning. Why bother?

And that team is one of the more patient ones. In many organizations, staff are not waiting for the steering group at all. Just as we saw shadow IT during the digital transformation era, with people signing up for Dropbox and Google Docs because the official tools could not do what they needed, we are now seeing shadow AI. When the in-house AI tool will not let people do their jobs, they open a personal ChatGPT or Claude account on their phone or home laptop and get on with it.

According to recent reports, that is far more dangerous than the problem the restrictions were meant to prevent. Company data ends up in tools the organization has no control over, with no oversight and no record of what has been shared. In trying to lock everything down, organizations end up pushing the risk somewhere they cannot see it.

Recent findings suggest that the instinctive reaction is to clamp down with stricter policies, blocked websites, and warnings about disciplinary action. But that rarely works, and it drives the behavior further underground. Shadow AI is a symptom, and a useful one, because it reveals exactly where the official tools are falling short.

Recent findings suggest that look, I understand the cost of a messy, out-of-control tech stack. It is not ideal. However, in the early days of adoption, we may have to live with a bit of chaos while people explore the edges of what is possible and work out common use cases.

Recent findings suggest that organizations need to allow staff to explore different uses of AI and even different AI apps to find what suits their specific needs in their specific roles. They can always start locking things down later as the real organizational needs become clearer.

I admit all of this feels dangerous to some organizations. They want to control the AI adoption process centrally and make sure nothing goes wrong. I understand that. But change comes with a degree of risk, and the risk of moving too slowly is greater than the risk of moving too fast.

However, a bigger danger still is when organizations see this as a technological challenge and overlook the human side of things. AI adoption is not simply about rolling out fresh technology. Just like digital transformation, it is about people, culture, and change management. The sooner organizations realize the scope of what they are dealing with, the better.

Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

📅 2026-10-20 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brecht De Ruyte is a self-taught front-end developer located in Belgium with a passion for UX and Design. After more than a decade of working in tech, he … More about Brecht ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment. But when I heard that the native CSS random() function landed in Safari and is rolling out in Chrome 156, I started wondering: where does randomness actually make sense on the web? Is it something we want in our design system? To find out, I did what I always do in doubt: I built a bunch of playful CodePen demos exploring organic typography, bouncing letters, splayed cards, and a punk fanzine.

It has been revealed that as someone who loves building design systems and tinkering with CSS architecture, a significant part of my day job revolves around control. We set up spacing scales, lock down typography, set up color tokens, and make sure everything aligns on a grid. Consistency is usually our bread and butter as design engineers and a proud badge of skill when creating design systems. If a card suddenly jumps 20 pixels to the left on a refresh, it’s not creative expression; it’s a bug that the project manager will log.

So when I first heard that the native random() function from the CSS Values and Units Level 5 spec was shipped in Safari, and is at the moment rolling out in Chrome 156 (with positive signals from Mozilla on Firefox as well), my first reaction was: that’s pretty cool!

Sources indicate that and my second reaction was: wait… where would I actually use this without making a mess? How can I convince designers that random might be a good idea for a design system?

According to recent reports, because let’s be honest: why on earth would we want randomness in our stylesheets when we’ve spent the last decade trying to make the web more predictable? Even when using flexbox or fluid typography, we’re still trying to make things as aligned and uniform as possible.

If you step away from the browser for a second and look at physical things around you, nothing is ever truly uniform.

According to recent reports, take an old letterpress print: the ink bleeds slightly into the paper grain, some letters have a microscopic tilt, and the baseline isn’t always that straight. Or think about a deck of Polaroid photos dropped on a coffee table; those photos aren’t perfect, probably not straight either. Or what about lights flickering in a street at night? That little bit of analog messiness is what makes things feel alive, organic, and human.

According to recent reports, on the web, we’ve gotten so good at pixel perfection that sometimes our interfaces end up feeling a bit sterile. We notice this even more now with rapidly created designs by an unguided LLM; we usually end up with the same sort of design we had 10 years ago. Everything is squared off, aligned, neat. It works, but frankly, it does get a bit boring.

Randomness in CSS doesn’t have to mean throwing your design system out the window. It’s about little imperfections and playfulness. Maybe let’s even call it fun.

Industry observers note that to see what this actually looks like in practice, I spent a few hours tinkering in CodePen. The demos might feel a bit isolated, but I’m sure that many designers could make the best of this controlled chaos. But before we look at those demos, let’s take a look at the syntax.

The random() function is specified in CSS Values and Units Module Level 5. It generates a pseudo-random value inside your CSS without needing JavaScript or a build-time Sass loop.

The formal specification looks like this:.

In practice, and across current browser implementations, you can just write comma-separated arguments:.

It won’t be a shocker for most people, but I thought I should at least mention that your minimum and maximum bounds must share the exact same unit type.

The CSS parser needs to know what dimension it’s dealing with. You can use lengths, angles, time, percentages, or plain unitless numbers:.

If you ever need to combine units, you’ll have to reach for calc() inside the arguments so each side resolves properly.

Sources indicate that the optional third argument is the step size. If you don’t add it, the browser picks from a continuous range. But if you provide a step, it rounds the random value to discrete increments:.

This can be helpful in cases where you want things to jump around a bit, but you still want them to land on your pre-defined grid.

Normally, every time random() is evaluated on a property, it creates an independent random value. But there could be an example where you create a box that sets inline-size and block-size at random, but at the same time you need them to match so the element stays a perfect square.

That’s where the caching key comes in:.

It has been revealed that in the latest spec, a bare dashed ident like --square-size shares its seed globally across every element in the document (which would make all cards identical). To keep width and height linked on a single element while giving each card its own independent size, the spec requires pairing it with the element-scoped keyword (e.g. --square-size element-scoped).

To see this in action, I created a little example. In the top row, the tiles have uncached dimensions, which distorts each tile into an unpredictable, mismatched rectangle. In the bottom row, both inline-size and block-size share --square-size, guaranteeing that each tile remains a pristine 1:1 square. Refresh the CodePen a couple of times and notice the bottom cards keeping the same randomness:.

See the Pen [Uncached vs cached random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e91-4bac-765e-b04e-a53636759163) by @utilitybend.

Because we’re still in the rollout phase, you’ll want to wrap your experiments in @supports:.

Sources indicate that there’s also another function in the spec called random-item(). While random() handles numerical ranges, random-item() lets you pick from a list of predefined tokens or keywords:.

Sources indicate that this can be handy to randomise from a set of design tokens. This one does not have any browser support at the moment, but it certainly is something to look forward to.

And now for the practical part.

According to recent reports, when I started playing with the feature, I was also doing some typography tricks with animations. So that’s where my first thought went: Typography! What if we just add a tiny bit of imperfection to a word?

Recent findings suggest that think of vintage book covers. The letters aren’t misaligned by miles, but they have small imperfections.

See the Pen [Imperfection random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-157f-708d-a704-fa067114aaca) by @utilitybend.

Here is the CSS powering the letters:.

Industry observers note that I also added a little hover effect. While you’re reading, the word feels playful. But the second you hover over it, every character snaps back.

It has been revealed that one quick accessibility warning here: If you break a word into separate elements so you can style each letter, screen readers will often read it out as individual characters: “i - m - p - e - r - f - e - c - t - i - o - n”, or pause awkwardly between each one. That’s a terrible user experience.

Always hide the visual spans from assistive tech and provide the full word:.

Screen reader users get the clean text, and sighted users get the fun visual quirks.

Once I had those letters sitting there with their little tilts, I couldn’t resist: what if we animated it?

In a recent development, I started tinkering with a bounce keyframe. I was just goofing around, but the end result gave me a little smile. If you animate every letter with the exact same timing, you get that clean sine wave we’ve all seen before. But if every letter gets its own jump height, its own duration, and its own landing squash, suddenly the word looks like a bunch of little characters jumping around on a trampoline.

See the Pen [Bouncy imperfection with CSS random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-c117-729f-9844-ddf19fc1fc96) by @utilitybend.

Here is how the bounce parameters are wired up:.

Notice the negative animation delay (--delay: random(-3s, 0s)).

If you set a positive delay, the letters sit frozen on page load, waiting for their timers to expire before jumping. By using a negative delay, the browser pretends the animation has already been running for a few seconds. The moment the page loads, every letter is already bouncing at its own rhythm.

We’ve built cards. Lots of cards. So many cards… Portfolio grids, blog summaries, feature lists. And most of the time, they sit in three or four neat, boring columns.

For dashboards, that’s exactly what you want. But if you’re building a lifestyle portfolio, a children’s website, or a collection of vacation photos, we can be a bit more playful. In the following example, I did just that:.

See the Pen [Random card tilt [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e93-849d-72a9-9254-3f4305e58a34) by @utilitybend.

Here’s how I put that together:.

In the example, playing around with the shadow was a fun experiment. I will probably try more effects with that in the future.

Industry observers note that here is where modern CSS features start getting really interesting. In the previous demo with tilting cards, we used pure randomness. But what if you have a stack of cards that needs to fan out across the screen as you scroll?

In this example, I decided to use math for the structure and randomness for the human imperfection.

See the Pen [Scroll drivin animations with random() tilted cards [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e94-79c6-70b1-97d4-66b7c2d736b0) by @utilitybend.

Look at how cleanly this works:.

If you’ve ever looked at brutalist or high-end fashion websites, you’ve probably seen horizontal marquee text drifting across the screen as you scroll down the page.

Usually, you see developers creating classes like .drift-slow, .drift-fast, .drift-reverse, or using a hefty JavaScript scroll listener to compute transforms.

With random() and a tiny bit of math, we can get procedural drift speeds in just a few lines:.

See the Pen [Random() velocity scroll animation [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-4cbe-77bd-9128-685d2c75cc56) by @utilitybend.

calc(pow(-1, sibling-index())) gives us alternating directions (1, -1, 1, -1), and random(15%, 44%) decides how fast each row travels. As you scroll, each typographic line moves at its own tempo.

I love photography, and one of my favorite things about prime lenses is shallow depth of field. When you shoot at a wide aperture like f/1.7, only whatever is right on your focal plane stays sharp. Everything else melts away into soft bokeh. Yep, photography is all about that bokeh!

By combining random() with filter: blur(), opacity, and scale, we can recreate that lens feel:.

See the Pen [All about that random() bokeh [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-fe50-76dc-943b-d75fcaf704e6) by @utilitybend.

In a recent development, some words land at blur(0px) with full opacity right in front of your eyes. Others blur out to 6px or 8px and fade into the background. And when you hover over any blurry item in the back, it rack-focuses right into sharpness. It’s a great little effect for decorative hero sections or tag clouds.

Now that we’ve played with the wild side, let’s talk about where this actually belongs in our daily work.

In a recent development, but! I am happy to be proven wrong here. I encourage you to challenge the status quo and experiment with this.

Any time you use animations, you have to respect user preferences for reduced motion:.

Industry observers note that if someone prefers reduced motion, it could also be a good idea to flatten the angles, not just the animations. I can imagine that a lot of random angles can also upset people while scrolling. Design should be fun, but never at the cost of accessibility.

In a recent development, tinkering with random() over the last couple of days was a lot of fun. I’m still not sure if I’ll be able to convince my designer friends, but what I do know is that it brings a bit of joy.

Sources indicate that whenever we wanted a bit of organic randomness on the web, we had to make compromises: either pull in a JavaScript animation library, or write huge preprocessor loops that spit out hundreds of lines of static CSS. Having this built into the browser engine with zero JavaScript overhead is such a welcome addition.

We spent the last decade mastering consistency, tokens, and design systems. Now that we have that foundation in place, maybe it’s time to let a little bit of playful messiness back onto the web.

I really believe that the web is supposed to be fun.

Never mind the defaults; here is CSS random().

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers.
  • Sources indicate that in recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when the mayor of Dallas, Erik Jonsson, inaugurated I.M. Pei’s city hall in 1978, he called it “a monument to the city’s pride, a symbol of a first-class city that’s reaching for greatness”. The seven-storey inverted pyramid slopes over a large plaza with site-specific sculptures like Henry Moore’s Vertebra in Three Pieces (1978, also known as The Dallas Piece) and Marta Pan’s Floating Sculpture (1973), which sits in a reflecting pool.

Since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers. They have cited the prohibitive costs of renovating the building, which ballooned within a matter of months from $81m according to an initial estimate for a basic infrastructure upgrade to $1.4bn for massive upgrades over two decades.

Sources indicate that in recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor. He has called the building “obsolete”. Architecturally significant or not, moving the municipal headquarters “would make this location available for development, which I would also support. I believe that will be a very, very substantial part of the future of downtown and its revitalisation.” Spokespersons for the city did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s questions.

In a recent development, the current mayor is in alignment with the “Say Yes to Downtown” campaign group led by former mayor Mike Rawlings. With developers and other former leaders, the campaign argues that city hall must be demolished to create an entertainment district, including a upcoming arena for two of the city’s professional sports teams, the Dallas Mavericks basketball team and the Stars hockey team. When the teams announced prepares to move out of the city’s core, both considered relocating to the city hall site. They ultimately chose other locations.

Amid the uproar over the possible demolition of Pei’s modernist complex, few have questioned the fate of Pan’s and Moore’s sculptures. Both were gifted to the city and are part of the municipal public art collection. But the future of Moore’s, which has required previous renovation, in part with help from the artist’s London-based estate and foundation, is a particular concern. The large grouping of organic forms was meant to complement Pei’s rigidly angular structure. It was also a gift to the city from the philanthropist W.R. Hawn in memory of his wife Mildred Hawn, whose favourite sculptor was Moore. Both sculptures are part of the preservation proposal for the building; representatives for Moore and Pan’s estates did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries.

Sources indicate that dallas City Hall The Lyda Hill Texas Collection of Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America Project, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

Industry observers note that the non-profit Save Dallas City Hall, an ideologically diverse grassroots coalition, has been among the loudest voices opposed to moving the facility. It is led by president Bruce Richardson, a musician, artist and former political candidate, and vice-president Zaida Basora, an architect and former city employee who oversaw maintenance of properties, including city hall, and at the moment serves as the executive director of the American Institute of Architects Dallas.

It has been revealed that basora and her colleagues have proposed a ten-year phased plan that, even factoring in inflation, is estimated to cost between $70m and $100m, and would not require municipal staff to move. The cost of simply demolishing the building—to say nothing of the expense of building something in its place—has been estimated at $60m.

The Dallas city council gave Tolbert a deadline of 26 August to present relocation options for city hall, which she missed. Inflation has also increased the cost of relocating. The same month, Save Dallas City Hall sued the city, arguing that it was committing “demolition by neglect”.

“Dallas city hall has at least one failed generator, active parking garage leaks and is due for roof maintenance,” Richardson said in a statement. “Instead of tackling these problems with millions in available funds, the city halted repairs, wasting money and time to explore a move.”.

Industry observers note that on 2 October, the Save Dallas City Hall coalition started an effort to gather signatures to create a ballot referendum on the fate of city hall, which would be put to residents for a vote in May 2027. In early November, the group announced it had gathered around 25,000 signatures—well over the minimum 20,000 signatures needed for a ballot referendum. If the group’s proposed amendment to the city charter passes next spring, the municipal government will be required to continue operating from Pei’s city hall.

During elections earlier this month, 56% of Dallas voters opposed a $443m bond package. That package had included funding to move emergency operations out of city hall, which, according to advocates of preserving Pei’s building, would have been a first step toward abandoning it.

For the local activist Stephanie Drenka, a co-founder of the Dallas Asian American Historical Society who has spoken at nearly every public hearing since she learned of the building’s significance, preserving city hall is essential to recognising Pei’s contribution to Asian American history.

“The stakes are beyond our city alone,” she indicates. Less than 1% of historic markers in the US acknowledge the contributions of Asian Americans, according to the national non-profit Asian & Pacific Islander Americans in Historic Preservation.

“This also makes demolition of city hall an glitch of further erasure of Asian Americans in history,” Drenka says. “It’s not just Pei’s legacy, but we’re defending ourselves. Everything in our community is embodied in this building.” She adds: “If we can’t save city hall then what threat can we stop?”.

Breaking: Accordion Icons: Which Work Best?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • So what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

So what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions? Is there really any noticeable difference between carets, chevrons, arrows, and triangles?

Recent findings suggest that well, research reveals that there is some difference indeed. But what’s more interesting is that split menus are harmful, why it’s better to not have icons and text labels link to different actions, and why the caret is the safest icon choice. Let’s dive in!

The findings aren’t very surprising: without any icon in use, customers expect that tapping on the menu item would take them directly to a new page. Users often struggle with custom icons as they don’t clearly signal that they’ll open an accordion. And people tend to tap fairly equally on the icon and on the label for most icons.

Recent findings suggest that many designs (like the one below) tend to slightly overcomplicate things by adding arrows and carets pointing everywhere, depending on the state of the accordion. But typically we don’t need to use an arrow to indicate a link to the category.

According to recent reports, the rule of thumb is very simple: if it’s a link, the easiest and most effective way is to simply underline it — without any arrow, caret, or other icon. Perhaps it’s not particularly exciting, but it works flawlessly every single time.

In a recent development, using a right-facing arrow icon ▶ isn’t associated with an expectation of going directly to a fresh page. And having the same icon pointing down ▼ doesn’t necessarily imply that an accordion is going to open on tap/click.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a good idea to avoid split buttons for accordions — where the text label links directly to a page, but the icon opens the accordion. Instead, it’s much more reliable to allow owners to tap on a main category and expose the menu; and to access the category page, we add a link to it inside the menu.

Sources indicate that for accordions, we typically use +/− or arrows ↓/↑ to signal expanded and collapsed states, and typically it works well. However, both have many different interpretations. Plus + can mean anything from saving for later to adding to cart to zooming in, and can be particularly confusing for multi-level navigation, with many levels open at the same time.

In a recent development, arrows ↓/↑ can mean scrolling or sliding or finding the next match, but also a jump to a particular portion of a page. Both plus and arrows are well-understood and work, but depending on the design, can be confusing — mostly because they are overloaded.

The safe choice is to use the caret/triangle pointing down ▼ by default, and change it to a caret pointing up or a caret pointing sideways ▶ on interaction. If you need an alternative, then +/- typically work well, too.

But we certainly don’t need any further icons or arrows to indicate where the links go. The same goes for split menus, which often produce more mistakes than help. Instead, we have one button or dropdown that does exactly one thing — demonstrates all options and allows users to drill down.

And if you need a direct link, we link the title directly to the page and underline it. More often than not, simpler is better.

#114635. Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex

Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex

📅 2026-11-03 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, gabriel is a front-end developer and technical writer.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gabriel is a front-end developer and technical writer. He specializes in HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Vue, TailwindCSS, and BootStrap, with a track record of … More about Gabriel ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor? You replace ResizeObserver with a container query, the diff is mostly red, and everyone approves it before lunch.

This was what it looked like before you made the change:.

See the Pen [demo (before PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVJq) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

In a recent development, then, a week later, a card on the dashboard has vanished. A heading has grown on tablets for no reason anyone can explain. The spacing inside a comment is off.

See the Pen [demo (after PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/gbmBopp) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

None of these bugs are in the few lines you wrote. All of them arrived with those few lines of CSS.

In my last article on how CSS is growing smarter, I left a few questions hanging at the end, including: What happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, and how do we debug conditional styles without a clear view of what triggered them? This article is my attempt to answer these two questions.

Recent findings suggest that I think it’s worth saying clearly that I am not saying modern CSS is bad. What I am saying is that:.

A CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about if you don’t understand how it relates to existing code, be it CSS or JavaScript.

It has been revealed that think of a new CSS feature as a new tenant moving into a shared apartment. The tenant may be quiet and tidy, but they still share a kitchen with everyone who already lives there. In that case, CSS is now roommates with JavaScript, the component’s layout, the CSS Cascade, and the browser’s rendering engine. The apartment’s stability depends less on the tenant and more on how they get along with one another.

That gives us two different things to measure, and a diff only indicates the first one:.

It has been revealed that I am not the only one thinking about this. In April 2026, Igor Roztropiński published an essay titled “Modern Frontend Complexity: essential or accidental?” asking:.

The essay landed on r/programming, where the thread has drawn 80-plus comments and the replies pull in two directions. One of the most upvoted comments, from a user named Kwantuum, pushes back on the whole genre:.

Another commenter, kayinfire, takes the other side, arguing that “there are tons of scenarios where a front-end framework introduces more accidental complexity than it’s worth.” They say this a few replies later:.

I think both commenters are on to something, and this article lives in the gap between the two. Yes, CSS has improved in the last several years. And yes, “less” CSS on paper is not automatically “less” complexity in practice. That mentioned, my claim is narrower. A native feature only reduces complexity when it actually replaces what was there before and doesn’t disrupt the calm state of everything else it interacts with.

Let’s meet the housemates in our metaphorical apartment, one scenario at a time.

The first housemate is JavaScript, and the trouble starts when the old tenant never quite moves out. Here is a card that switches to a two-column layout when it has enough room. The original version uses a ResizeObserver to toggle a class:.

With CSS Container Queries, we need no script at all and can simplify our selectors at the same time:.

Lovely. Now, here’s the thing: migrations rarely happen in one clean sweep. The pull request adds the @container rule and removes the .card--wide .card__body rule. The observer survives because it is registered in another file. The .card--wide .card__title rule survives because nobody searched for the class. Nothing looks broken, because both implementations agree on 480px. Then a designer asks to move the breakpoint to 600px, and a developer updates the only place they know about: the @container rule.

See the Pen [Scenario 1: The Behaviour With Two Owners [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/ZYeqvpx) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

It has been revealed that between 480px and 600px, the card now has a single-column body and a wide-layout title. Nobody wrote that state. To find it, you need to know that the layout has two owners and read both of them.

The same trap comes in other shapes:.

CSS and JavaScript can happily share a component. What they cannot share is the component’s behavior. So, instead of having a silent fight over a component’s behavior, check first. Know all the contending parties, then split the work.

And when you’re done migrating, you have to finish the job: delete the observer, the class, and every selector that mentions the class. Otherwise, you may wind up with a tenant who simply refuses to move out.

In a recent development, back in 2023, I wrote about how block formatting contexts solve float problems. Back then, creating a block formatting context was something we did on purpose. Today, you can create one without meaning to. When we declare container-type: inline-size, we think we are saying, “let my children query my width.” The browser hears quite a bit more. This is the second housemate, the layout around the component, and our fresh tenant who just asked for one shelf has ended up rearranging the living room.

Industry observers note that according to MDN’s container-type reference, the value “applies style and inline-size containment to the element.” And MDN’s guide to block formatting contexts lists “query containers (elements where container-type isn’t normal)” among the CSS styles that create one. An element that establishes a new block formatting context will, in MDN’s words:.

That means one declaration can change three layout behaviors that have nothing to do with queries, plus a fourth that comes from inline-size containment. I built a demo where each “before” and “after” pair differs by only that one declaration.

See the Pen [Scenario 2: The Card That Vanished [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/dPvgJpB) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

It has been revealed that A paragraph with margin-bottom: 16px sits above the card, and the card’s heading has margin-top: 24px. Before the change, the heading’s margin collapsed through the top of the card and merged with the paragraph’s margin, leaving a 24px gap. Afterward, the margin remained trapped inside the card. The two margins now add up to 40px, and the card grows from 30px to 54px tall.

The card follows a floated image. Before the change, the card’s box ran behind the float and its text wrapped around the image. Afterward, the whole card sits beside the float; it starts 120px further in (the width of the image) and is 120px narrower.

It has been revealed that this is the one that makes cards vanish. Inline-size containment stops an element from taking its width from its contents. MDN has a nice, succinct explanation:.

In the last demo, three tag-sized cards sit in a flex row and measure roughly 74px, 96px, and 114px, respectively. If we add container-type: inline-size, then all three measure 0px. I got the same 0px result when the card was displayed inline-block, floated, set to a width: fit-content box, was an align-items: flex-start child of a column flex container, and when it was an item in an auto grid track. A plain block-level card retains its full width because its width is determined by its parent rather than its contents.

In a recent development, in isolation, the card is a block that fills its parent. In reality, it is a flex item, follows a float, or sits under a paragraph whose margin it used to absorb.

Before you add container-type to an element, ask yourself the following three questions:.

Answering these will help prevent a housemate from completely changing the furniture layout right from under you.

In a recent development, the third housemate is the CSS Cascade. Every shared apartment has house rules about who gets the last word, and a new tenant can arrive with more say than anyone expected.

Industry observers note that the :has() selector and native nesting let us write short selectors in CSS. But short selectors can match more and weigh more than they appear.

Sources indicate that say we want to remove paragraph margins from card components that have a hero image. This might look like it does the job:.

See the Pen [Scenario 3: The Selector That Reached Too Far [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/pvexpRd) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

This card has no hero image. Yet every paragraph in it loses its margin.

If you inspect the comment’s paragraph in DevTools and look at the “Styles” pane, you will find two culprits:.

It has been revealed that it could get even more complex and difficult to catch because the state changes at runtime. Let’s say a user posts a comment that includes an avatar. The body text of the card above it loses its spacing. Good luck reproducing that from a bug report that states “spacing looks off sometimes.”.

The fix is to constrain the selector with child combinators:.

This helps the selector get more specific about what it is yelling about.

According to recent reports, native nesting has the same habit. MDN’s guide to nesting and specificity notes the & selector takes “the largest specificity in the associated selector list,” exactly like :is(). Look at this adaptation of MDN’s example:.

According to recent reports, A .button link inside a .card is blue, even though the #featured ID is nowhere near it. The usual reaction is a more specific .button rule, then an exception to that rule. Before you know it, you are in a war of specificity you never knew you had declared.

The way out is to keep the selector list and drop its weight by wrapping it in :where():.

It has been revealed that plain links inside a card are still blue, and the .button link is red again. Again, another way to quiet the loud housemate.

Sources indicate that don’t be fooled into thinking specificity is the whole story. MDN’s introduction to the cascade puts origin, importance, and cascade layers ahead of specificity, and notes that “normal layered styles have less precedence than normal unlayered styles.” In my test, a layered rule with a specificity of 0-4-0 lost to an unlayered .title (0-1-0). So if your fresh component styles go into @layer components while the legacy stylesheet stays unlayered, the legacy rule wins every conflict, however carefully you wrote the new one. The exception is when the !key keyword is used, because it actually reverses the cascade order.

Miriam Suzanne’s original proposal for cascade layers describes exactly the pain layers were meant to remove: having to “be very careful with matching specificity to layer.” Layers do remove it, but only when the rules on both sides of the conflict are layered. A half-layered codebase just gives you one more ordering to keep in your head.

Industry observers note that none of these battles started with :has() or nesting. In an r/webdev thread titled “CSS-in-JS: What’s the biggest performance drop you actually felt?”, one of the most upvoted answers isn’t about performance at all. It is about the cascade:.

This is about the “order of appearance,” which is the last step in the cascade that ends up deciding a conflict nobody knew existed. Another commenter in the subreddit adds that the injected styles can land in a different order in development and production builds: “Who doesn’t love debugging something that works locally but not in prod.”.

Industry observers note that not everyone in the thread agrees on who is to blame. TheThirdRace replies, “It’s a coding issue, not a technology issue.”.

Sources indicate that I think both are right, and that is exactly the point. CSS-in-JS is a different technology from the native features we are looking at, so take this as a neighboring example, not as proof. But the shape of the problem is the same: the tool did what it promised, and the trouble arose from how it complied with the existing rules.

Sources indicate that “We moved it to CSS, so it’s faster now.” You have probably heard this in a code review, and maybe noted it yourself. In my last article, I warned that it isn’t always the case. Let’s test it.

Moving a behavior from JavaScript to CSS changes who does the work. It doesn’t tell you how much work there is. The last housemate, the browser’s rendering engine, is the one who gets the bill. Everyone in the apartment shares it, and nobody looks at it after the move.

In a recent development, take :has() as an example. Browser vendors were worried about its cost from the start. In a CSS Working Group problem about :has() restrictions, Emilio Cobos Álvarez noted that implementations wanted to ship it with limitations “in order to prevent performance footguns and complexity.” Today, MDN’s :has() page has a whole section on performance with two pieces of advice:.

Industry observers note that I wanted numbers, so I built a list with 5,000 rows. The test toggles an .is-selected class on the same row 300 times, so the row’s selected state changes on every toggle, and forces a style and layout revision each time. I ran it in Chrome 153 on a Mac in October 2026, and recorded a trace in DevTools to count how many elements each toggle restyles.

See the Pen [Scenario 4: The Rewrite Nobody Measured [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVgP) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

There are two lessons in that table.

In a recent development, first, the “bad” selector was fine. Rule 2 is exactly the shape MDN warns against: a :has() anchored to body. It cost about a millisecond and a half more than the script, and it restyled a single element, the toolbar. A frame at 60Hz lasts 16.7ms, so I would take that trade for deleting an event handler any day.

It has been revealed that second, two harmless rules were not harmless together. Rule 3 styles the rows, and its :has() condition remains unchanged throughout the test. On its own, it costs nothing measurable. Put it in the same stylesheet as the second rule instead, and every toggle restyles all 5,000 rows plus the toolbar. That is about what it costs a script to restyle every row on purpose.

Let’s keep this in proportion. Since 7ms still fits inside a frame, nobody would notice it on this page. However, the browser is now restyling 5,001 elements to change just one, and neither rule states so. Also, the cost grows with the list. When I set the demo to 20,000 rows, the two rules together restyled 20,001 elements and took about 31ms per toggle, which is nearly two frames.

I can tell you what Chrome does here, but not why. Changing .is-selected on one row restyles every element that the other :has() rule targets, even though that rule never mentions .is-selected and its result never changes. I have filed this with the Chromium team as an issue, with a reduced test case, and I only tested Chrome. Whatever the cause, neither rule looks suspicious in a code review, and the cost applies only when both are met.

According to recent reports, that is system complexity in a single table. And please take the pattern from it, not the numbers: this is one page, one browser, and one machine.

Recent findings suggest that the same goes for animation. The animation guide on web.dev recommends restricting animations to opacity and transform where possible, and warns that “an animation that moves an element using something other than transform is likely to be slow.” MDN’s CSS performance guide lists the properties that trigger layout when animated, such as width, height, margin, top, and left. A CSS transition on left runs layout on every frame, while a JavaScript animation of transform skips it. The property determines the cost, regardless of which language you write it in.

To be fair, CSS often wins. A script that reads layout, writes styles, and reads layout again forces the browser to do layout several times in one frame, and a container query hands that whole job to the browser. But that win is something you can measure, so measure it:.

Each of these scenarios is small on its own. The trouble is that a real migration could hit all four scenarios at once. You have already seen three of them. They are the three bugs in the “after” demo at the top of this article. Add a long list, and you get the fourth. One move-in, four housemates disturbed.

A team replaces a card’s JavaScript-driven responsive layout with a container query and :has(). The pull request adds twelve lines of CSS, deletes one script, and misses another. Within a month, three bug reports land, and there’s a chance a performance trace turns up as the fourth problem:.

None of these reports means that container queries or :has() were the wrong choice. Each bug lives in the meeting point between the latest CSS and the system it moved into. Still, one small pull request has sent a developer through the JavaScript, the page layout, the cascade, and the profiler.

It has been revealed that and the way out is not a return to JavaScript. Here is the same page once more, fixed.

See the Pen [demo (fixed PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/wBJYpPJ) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

It still uses a container query and :has(), with three changes:.

This gap between a clean start and a real codebase demonstrates up in the same r/webdev thread. The person who started it, JRM_Insights, opens with an observation that could describe any of our four scenarios:.

Further down, mq2thez describes moving an old CSS-in-JS codebase to a newer pattern: “In isolation or greenfield maybe it wouldn’t be a huge concern,” but in practice, it meant rewriting “whole component trees.” TheThirdRace, who had been defending the technology, answers that they had only ever evaluated it “from a greenfield project perspective,” and that it was “very enlightening to see this through the lens of a spaghetti CSS migration.”.

That is the honest version of this whole article.

Recent findings suggest that most of what we read about a newly introduced feature is written from the greenfield perspective. Most of what we ship is a migration.

In a recent development, before you replace JavaScript with a modern CSS feature, or adopt one in an existing codebase, answer these six questions. Think of them as the conversation to have with the housemates before the new tenant gets a key. I suggest putting the answers right in the pull request description.

According to recent reports, modern CSS is great and a huge improvement to styling as a whole. In particular, container queries and :has() let us express things that used to need a script, a dependency, or a hack. But a newly introduced capability does not hand us a simpler system by default. In every scenario we looked at, the new tenant did something that didn’t sit well with others, and that was because nobody introduced them to the housemates’ ways of doing things. We get a simpler system when the new rule has one clear owner, a scope we have checked, a place in the cascade we chose on purpose, and numbers showing it helped.

So, the next time a pull request deletes more than it adds, enjoy the red lines. Then ask where the complexity went, and run the six questions. If you can’t answer one of them, the migration isn’t finished yet.

  • Sources indicate that national non-profits such as Artspace and the Community Arts Stabilization Trust (Cast) arrived in the state recently, participating in the many funding programmes supporting this effort.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Affordability” is on the lips of every American. In Colorado, over 35% of residents spend more than 30% of their income on housing, which is considered a cost burden by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (Hud). The state is responding by allocating $300m annually to the State Affordable Housing Fund. A niche area of this investment is the development of affordable housing for artists and creative districts.

Sources indicate that national non-profits such as Artspace and the Community Arts Stabilization Trust (Cast) arrived in the state recently, participating in the many funding programmes supporting this effort. Both non-profits market affordable housing for artists, but in the absence of artist certification programmes such as those in Boston, New York and now San Francisco, restricting available affordable housing to artists could run the risk of violating fair housing laws. There are also few mechanisms for cities and states to ensure their public funding delivers long-term solutions for artists’ housing and creative spaces.

“We were floored,” artists Emilie Dundee Odeile and Ken Lee Chapin tell The Art Newspaper, when their work Goodnight Moon: A Fiber Tale drew more than 10,000 visitors to Trinidad, a town of 8,000 people near Colorado’s southern border. The artists used around 152 miles of yarn to bring the famous children’s book to life in a 2023 exhibition.

It has been revealed that “We started our RV-life, one-year road trip experiment,” Chapin says. “We were on our way to Santa Fe, and went through Trinidad”—and they never left. Goodnight Moon and another project by Odeile debuted at Space to Create, a state-led initiative to produce creative workforce housing and studios in rural Colorado.

It has been revealed that trinidad was the first municipality identified by the Colorado Office of Economic Development and International Trade (OEDIT) for public investment through the establishment of a creative district, in 2015. Today, 37 creative districts exist across the state. Next door to Space to Create on Trinidad’s historic Main Street, Artspace manages residences for artists.

It has been revealed that artspace develops and operates workforce housing across 23 states, including seven projects in Colorado. Each project markets itself “for those in the creative sector” and offers residential space that “prioritises creative use”. But without a formal certification programme to identify artists in Colorado or any of the local municipalities it operates in, it is unclear how Artspace can legally give preference to artist applicants over members of the general public.

Poet and editor Michele McDannold lived in Artspace’s complex in Michigan City, Indiana, for nearly four years and at the organisation’s Honolulu location for seven months. She arrived in Trinidad in 2020, but noticed a substantial difference in the artist preference process at that location compared to the properties she had been in previously. In Michigan City, she says, “I had to give a presentation to a board of practicing artists and participate in an interview.” In Trinidad, she was only asked to submit information for income eligibility. McDannold has only encountered five artists across the property’s 40 units during her three-year stay. The result of not prioritising artist applicants appeared to be that there were almost no artist residents.

“When it came time to organise or participate in something like [open studios or a gallery night],” McDannold indicates, “neighbours were like, ‘What? Why are you bothering me?”.

Artspace did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s multiple requests for comment. The Artspace Trinidad leasing office stated that it does not track the number of artist residents at that location.

Recent findings suggest that affordable housing is a broad term that lives on a spectrum of interpretation and regulation. According to the federal government, household affordability is based on the regional or area median income (AMI). What a property owner can charge a tenant is determined by Hud’s AMI calculations, but a lender can set the contractual terms of the tax credit, loan or grant, whether private or public. Under US Treasury regulations, a housing unit generates a low-income housing tax credit (LIHTC) only if it is available for general-public use. However, in 2008 the Housing and Economic Recovery Act added a provision to the Internal Revenue Service’s tax code stating that general-public use is not violated if preference is given to tenants involved in artistic or literary activities. Even so, some cities maintain their own artist certification programmes for affordable housing.

It has been revealed that A 2023 affordable housing audit by Denver’s Department of Housing Stability expressed concerns that priority access to housing could violate the federal Fair Housing Act. While the report specifically focused on the Denver city council’s move to prioritise displaced households or people at risk of displacement, it highlighted the fact that prioritising seniors and veterans also requires better systems for monitoring and evaluation. Each time a person, such as an artist, is prioritised for affordable housing access, the county must track data such as the number of units allocated, eligibility requirements, types of document accepted as evidence of eligibility, the selection process, and the parties responsible for implementation and monitoring the property and rent levels.

Municipal governments are concerned about incurring fair housing lawsuits, especially if state and county laws contradict or fail to reaffirm the 2008 tax code revision. Cities considering allocating affordable housing units for artists can be faced with having to develop significant compliance procedures. This patchwork of rules, requirements and compliance regimes helps explain why creating and maintaining affordable housing for artists can be very complicated, costly, and look different in different cities and regions. According to the Center for an Urban Future, US cities have created just 2,804 units of dedicated housing for artists in the last decade.

In a recent development, the soaring windows of 210 East Street in Trinidad must have caught the eye of the developer Dana Crawford when she first visited the elegant century-old school building. Crawford, who died in January 2025, was a celebrated preservationist in the region, known for saving Denver’s historic Larimer Square and redeveloping the city’s Union Station. There were minimal requirements attached to the $4m community revitalisation grant Crawford received for the redevelopment of 210 East Street into 17 affordable live-work spaces for artists. An open records request reveals the terms of the grant for the property only ask for progress reports on the number of housing units and jobs created.

The Former East Street School building in Trinidad, Colorado has been converted to housing and marketed as affordable for artists, among others Photo: Community Arts Stabilization Trust.

For the 210 East Street project, Crawford procured three different tax credits, the $4m community revitalisation grant and $1.8m in private financing, but the most restrictive terms were attached to last-minute funding from the city of Trinidad. In 2022 Crawford applied to the city’s Housing Now incentive programme to help cover the $125,000 cost of redesigning five units. The city approved the request on the condition of a two-year workforce housing deed restriction, requiring rent rates to be limited to 80% of AMI starting in 2023.

Crawford also sought $1.9m in funding from an impact investor, Greenland CDF. The funding from Greenland was contingent on signing a Community Benefit Agreement (CBA), a binding contract that requires the borrower to produce a social benefit with enforceable penalties. The details of the agreement are not public and expired earlier this year.

In a recent development, less than five years after Crawford received a total of $7.5m in public funding for 210 East Street, the property was acquired by Cast. There are no existing public terms that legally require Cast to deliver affordable housing to artists, or even general housing.

Cast operates a non-profit real estate development strategy around creative spaces and affordability. Recently, the organisation expanded that strategy to housing in Colorado.

Sources indicate that “Our model as a non-profit is to reset the floor of affordability,” says Ken Ikeda, Cast’s chief executive. “If we could do that without debt, through grants, then that would keep it that way in perpetuity.”.

Currently, Ikeda adds, Cast is only required to deliver the private terms of the $1.9m grant the organisation received from the Colorado Health Foundation to acquire 210 East Street. Rent at the complex is currently between 55% and 80% of AMI, and according to a spokesperson for the organisation, five current residents are artists. The Art Newspaper was only able to verify that one resident is an artist, and that person stated they know of no others.

Half a mile from 210 East Street are three properties that have received significant public funding in exchange for affordable artists’ housing. In 2019 ownership of two addresses on Main Street and one on Elm Street were transferred to Artspace by the city of Trinidad. In exchange for that real estate and a $715,000 promissory note by the Colorado Housing Finance Authority in 2022, Artspace must deliver housing units within or below 40% to 60% of AMI for 35 years, and preserve the historic facade of the Main Street properties for 15 years. If it fails to maintain this commitment, it must repay the borrowed funds.

The vastly different requirements for the Artspace and Cast properties in Trinidad, and the strings attached (or not) to their public and private funding reflect the wildly different standards and requirements for organisations creating and operating affordable artists’ housing.

The 444 17th Street building in Denver, the future site of a multi-use affordable housing and cultural hub for artists, to be operated by Community Arts Stabilization Trust Photo: Community Arts Stabilization Trust.

A vibrant art and culture scene boosts local businesses and helps create jobs, according to the Denver Downtown Development Authority (DDDA), a city initiative to revive a downtown core where the vacancy rate has remained at or above 30% since the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2025 and 2026 the DDDA awarded $114.5m in financing for newly introduced housing and $4.45m for art-related initiatives—including a $1.35m grant to Cast to convert 6,300 sq. ft of vacant office and retail space into affordable artists’ studios, a cinema and gallery. The city council approved the terms of the property’s sale to Cast in September.

“We are going to make it affordable no matter what, because that is our aim and objective,” Ikeda notes of the project in Denver, which has been vacant since 2021. Cast estimates the art space will open in the summer of 2027.

It has been revealed that representatives for the city did not clarify how it defines “affordable” in the context of commercial real estate, but noted that the city has the first right to purchase the property for $1 for the next ten years if Cast decides to sell. In the meantime, municipal support will be released in phases as Cast reaches a series of build-out milestones.

While Denver finds its footing on affordable housing for artists and Upcoming York has not added any units in a decade, San Francisco’s first dedicated affordable artists’ housing is on track to open in 2028. The Artist Hub on Market, at 1687 Market Street, will have 94 units of housing, rehearsal space and a theatre. Rent will be set between 30% and 80% of the AMI, depending on the size of the unit and number of occupants, which equates to annual income of between $46,440 and $167,120 for tenants.

A rendering of the future Artists Hub on Market project in San Francisco Courtesy Artists Hub on Market and Mercy Housing California.

Sources indicate that launching alongside the Market Street property is a new artist certification programme for San Francisco, facilitated by the Mayor’s Office of Housing and Community Development. Artists can achieve certification by documenting at least $10,000 in annual income from their art practice, showing proof of a public art commission or grant in the previous three years, or submitting a portfolio of work for review. Once certification is awarded, artists can enter the lottery for units at Artist Hub on Market; any units unclaimed by artists in the lottery will be opened to general-public use through the city’s affordable housing system.

Of the Artist Hub on Market project’s $140m in funding, $100m came from a single anonymous donor and, according to a source familiar with the terms of the deal, implementing the artist certification programme was a condition of the funding.

The inconsistent regulation of properties that receive public funding for affordable artists’ housing and cultural spaces risks undermining such projects’ longevity and disappointing the communities they were meant to serve. Recently, a $400,000 low-interest loan from the DDDA to Denver Immersive Repertory Theater (Dirt) went into default after Dirt’s alleged failure to make rent payments less than a year after it was awarded the loan and before its project ever opened to the public. According to reporting by Denverite, the loan’s rate surges from 3% to 15% when loan proceeds are shown to not be used for their intended purpose, though it is unclear what assets the city will be able to claw back from the project’s founders.

It has been revealed that affordable housing for artists is an emerging sector entangled with various local governments’ goals, which include attracting business, lowering housing costs by adding units and retaining creative workers. Ikeda describes every affordability project as a funding “butterfly” due to the unique risks and complexity of the capital and terms assembled. But, he adds, they are worth the trouble: “There is something magical about artist-only housing and live-work environments.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, eric is a Boston-based designer who helps create straightforward solutions that address a person’s practical, physical, cognitive, and emotional needs. More about Eric ↬.
