📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the eighth edition of Frieze Los Angeles will welcome 102 exhibitors under the sprawling white tent on the grounds of the Santa Monica Airport. The exhibitor list, as in previous years, includes heavy local representation—with more than one-third of participants operating a space in Los Angeles.

According to recent reports, the roster includes established Los Angeles galleries such as Jeffrey Deitch, Regen Projects, David Kordansky, Château Shatto, Commonwealth and Council, Anat Ebgi, Night Gallery, the Pit and Roberts Projects. Four younger Los Angeles galleries will make their debuts in the Focus section for emerging galleries: Megan Mulrooney, Rajiv Menon Contemporary, House of Seiko and Zodiac Pictures. Erin Christovale from the Hammer Museum will curate this section.

In a recent development, international blue-chip galleries returning to Frieze Los Angeles include Gagosian, Hauser & Wirth, David Zwirner, Pace, White Cube, Perrotin, Gladstone, Almine Rech, Thaddaeus Ropac and Sprüth Magers. First-time exhibitors include Gallery Wendi Norris from San Francisco, Franklin Parrasch in New York, G Gallery in Seoul, Newchild in Antwerp, and Yehudi Hollander-Pappi and Danielian in Brazil.

A handful of prominent galleries will not be returning after taking part in recent editions, like Berggruen Gallery from San Francisco, Ortuzar and Tina Kim Gallery in New York, Mendes Wood DM and Nara Roesler from Brazil, Southern Guild from Cape Town and Timothy Taylor from London. Turnover year-over-year remains around 28% for a second consecutive year, amid stable overall exhibitor numbers.

Visitors to the fair will be greeted at the entrance by a newly introduced work by the Los Angeles-based artist rafa esparza called Queercancha, painted across two adobe panels mounted on chrome steel, drawing on Southern California’s culture of lowrider cruising.

Amid a boom following the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic, art dealers from all over the world began setting up shop in the Los Angeles area. However, many of those outposts have since closed alongside local dealerships—most recently, the Landing on Jefferson Boulevard. Along with a global market downturn, many local businesses were hurt by the devastating 2025 wildfires that nearly saw that year’s edition of Frieze Los Angeles cancelled. A handful of galleries have closed their local spaces and shifted their attentions to New York, including Southern Guild and Pietro Alexander.

This may be one of the final years the fair will be held at the Santa Monica Airport; the facility is scheduled to close permanently to aviation at the end of 2028 for conversion into a public park.

#114603. British Airways Avios — Short Nonstop Domestic Flights

British Airways Avios — Short Nonstop Domestic Flights

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes.
  • The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from Upcoming York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Industry observers note that most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA.

But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TIME has released its annual Top 100 Photos of the Year feature, celebrating striking images that capture the biggest moments and events of 2026. One of the featured photos was shot by acclaimed photographer and filmmaker Jimmy Chin using the iPhone 18 Pro, marking a milestone for Apple’s latest flagship smartphone and, of course, Chin himself.

Chin, an Academy Award-winning director, National Geographic photographer, and accomplished mountaineer, photographed his longtime climbing partner, Conrad Anker, as part of a upcoming series, What Holds Us. Chin and Anker have climbed together for 25 years, scaling peaks around the world.

“What I was after was that intersection: human ambition in pursuit of awe and wonder, set against a landscape that was here long before us and will be here long after,” Chin explains.

According to recent reports, “Out there you are reminded how small you are. That has always put things in perspective for me, and I hope it does for whoever is standing in front of the picture.”.

For Chin, who has shot in many extreme and remote locations throughout his career, the smaller and lighter the gear, the better.

“A production puts something between you and the person in front of you — gear, crew, the apparatus of a shoot. Working this way there was no apparatus. It was just the two of us, which is the only condition under which that kind of ease shows up in a frame,” Chin continues.

Using Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro, Chin was able to travel lighter without sacrificing performance or image quality. As his photo above reveals, the iPhone 18 Pro more than delivered — a testament to just how far smartphone imaging technology has come. Chin is far from the only photographer or filmmaker to integrate an iPhone into a professional workflow in recent years.

Chin shot 48MP ProRAW photos the iPhone 18 Pro and then stitched multiple shots to create one of his signature panoramas. The final photo is over 300 megapixels and 25,000 pixels wide. There’s no question it holds up extremely well in the large print featured in the What Holds Us exhibit.

Chin’s photos are also part of the What Holds Us exhibition, curated by Kathy Ryan, appearing alongside works by Alex Prager and Jack Davison. After debuting in New York City in September, the exhibition opens in London on December 4, running at Saatchi Yates Gallery through December 13.

  • According to recent reports, british photographer Timon Benson has received the RPS Award for Achievement in the Art of Photography (under 30).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Royal Photographic Society (RPS) has announced the recipients of its 2026 Awards, with cinematographer Sir Roger Deakins among this year’s honorees.

According to recent reports, deakins has received the RPS Centenary Medal, the Society’s most prestigious honor. Widely regarded as one of the greatest cinematographers in film history, Deakins has won two Academy Awards for Best Cinematography and five BAFTA Awards in the same category.

According to recent reports, british photographer Timon Benson has received the RPS Award for Achievement in the Art of Photography (under 30). At the beginning of his career, Benson was already attracting significant national and international recognition. His work spans documentary photography, choreography, and abstraction, exploring the nature of photography and its relationship with contemporary life.

The RPS Progress Medal in the Science of Photography has been awarded to Professor Marc Levoy, an American computer graphics researcher and Professor Emeritus of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University. Levoy is also a vice president and fellow at Adobe and a Distinguished Engineer at Google.

It has been revealed that british photographic artist Mandy Barker is the recipient of The RPS Award for Environmental Responsibility. Barker is internationally recognized for her work documenting marine plastic debris. Working alongside scientists, she uses photography to highlight the scale of plastic pollution in the world’s oceans and its impact on marine life and the wider environment.

Recent findings suggest that documentary photographer and filmmaker Polly Braden has received the RPS Award for Social Impact. Her long-term collaborative projects explore how people live and work, and their place in society. Her latest project, Against the Tide, produced with The Guardian, followed young people in 17 coastal towns. The project was exhibited at Arnolfini in Bristol and Firstsite in Colchester, and also brought 16 young people to Parliament to give evidence to MPs.

Now in its 148th year, the Royal Photographic Society Awards date back to 1878. The Society describes them as the world’s longest-running photography awards. They recognize achievements across still and moving images, celebrating individuals rather than individual photographs. The awards cover a broad range of disciplines, including moving image, fresh media, science and imaging, education, publishing, and curation.

Victoria Humphries, CEO of the Royal Photographic Society, notes the awards reflect the breadth of the photographic community and the many ways people contribute to the medium.

“The RPS Awards provide an opportunity to recognize and celebrate those who are making a difference, whether through their creativity, innovation, research, education or their contribution to the wider photographic community,” Humphries notes.

“As an organization, we believe that photography is for everyone, and these RPS Awards demonstrate that there are so many different ways to engage with, contribute to and shape its future.”.

Deakins says he is particularly pleased to be recognized for his still photography, given his career in cinematography.

Industry observers note that “I’m very honored to receive this award from the Royal Photographic Society. Although I have been more known for my work in cinematography, still photography has always been a passion and more personal to me. To be recognized by the Royal Photographic Society for my work in stills is amazing and means a great deal to me.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A rare cabinet photograph of the New York Giants, one of early professional baseball’s most significant teams, taken by renowned baseball photographer Joseph Hall in 1889, is up for auction.

It has been revealed that one of Major League Baseball’s oldest franchises, the New York Giants rose to prominence in the late 19th century, winning back-to-back championships in 1888 and 1889, before the modern World Series was established in 1903. The team boasted several future Baseball Hall of Famers during this era. Its legacy continues today as the San Francisco Giants, following the franchise’s relocation from New York to California in 1958.

The photograph, which is being offered by auction house Huggins & Scott as part of a sale which runs through December 3, features the Fresh York Giants team that won the 1888 World Championship. The auction house notes it has never handled another example of this particular photograph in its imperial cabinet format, making it one of the rarest of Joseph Hall’s baseball team photographs.

Industry observers note that hall photographed many of the Major League baseball teams in 1888 and was widely regarded as the leading baseball photographer of the late 1880s. Hall’s cabinet photographs of professional baseball teams and players are among the most sought-after photographic collectibles of the late 19th century, with his images of teams posing in uniform at ballparks commanding the highest prices.

While a smaller cabinet card featuring the same image of the Giants appeared at auction several years ago, Huggins & Scott indicates it cannot recall seeing another example of this photograph in this larger format. According to the auction house, the size and quality of the print are particularly noteworthy given the limitations of photographic production in the late 19th century. Producing photographs of this scale and quality required a considerable investment of time and resources, and the auction house suggests that only a small number of prints may have been made.

Industry observers note that unlike other photographs Hall took of the Giants that feature an outdoor stadium background, the image reveals 19 members of the team posing together in a studio. Among those pictured are six future Baseball Hall of Famers: Tim Keefe, Roger Connor, Buck Ewing, Jim O’Rourke, John Montgomery Ward, and Mickey Welch.

The photograph is up for sale in the Fall Auction at Huggins & Scott Auctions, which runs through December 3.

  • The winners were confirmed at an award ceremony at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London on the evening of 24 November.
  • Industry observers note that cultura en Vena, who has been awarded €40,000, will puts the funds towards its Arte Ambulatorio project, which brings reproductions of works of art and other forms of creative programming into hospital spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the charity Art Explora has revealed the five winners of the 2026 edition of its Académie des beaux-arts European Award, which recognises innovative work by non-profit arts and culture organisations in Europe. They are Polish performing arts foundation Jazdaa Polska!, Spanish art and health organisation Cultura en Vena, the French library charity Bibliothèques Sans Frontières, UK literary organisation London Writers Centre and Slovakian theatre tech giant RAMAGU. The organisations were awarded funds ranging from €30,000-50,000, shared from a total £180,000.

The winners were confirmed at an award ceremony at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London on the evening of 24 November. Each of them, apart from RAMAGU—which won an audience choice award—was selected by an international jury, which included several members of the Académie des beaux-arts in Paris, such as the illustrator Emmanuel Guibert and the sculptor Eva Jospin; Vanja Kaludjercic, the director of the International Film Festival Rotterdam; and Antonija Letinić, a cultural development consultant in Croatia. Frédéric Jousset, the French entrepreneur and founder of Art Explora, was also a juror.

Industry observers note that cultura en Vena, who has been awarded €40,000, will puts the funds towards its Arte Ambulatorio project, which brings reproductions of works of art and other forms of creative programming into hospital spaces. The newly introduced phase of the project will involve an exhibition inspired by the work of Frida Kahlo, as well as live music sessions and creative writing workshops for children. Previous Arte Ambulatorio interventions focused on the work of the Spanish artists Francisco Goya and Joaquín Sorolla.

According to the organisation, “Frida Kahlo’s artistic universe offers a powerful entry point into themes closely connected to the hospital experience: the body, pain, vulnerability, identity, resilience, emotional expression and care.”.

“Cultura en Vena takes art as seriously as care,” Jousset tells The Art Newspaper. He indicates the jury was convinced by “their rigour”. “They measure their impact and keep improving each exhibition based on patients’ and staff feedback,” he continues. “With over 23,000 peopkeople reached last year, they are one of the leading voices in arts and wellbeing in Spain.”.

Industry observers note that bibliothèques Sans Frontières, meanwhile, will put its €50,000 award towards its L’autre retour project. The initiative involves workshops within which Ukrainian veterans are invited to draw, read and write with members of their community outside of a clinical environment, in an effort to help with reintegration after the military. The charity then plans to tour some of the works in Ukraine, as well as show them at the European Commission in Brussels.

“This project indicates art as an act of rebuilding,” Jousset says.

The additional funded projects include developing touch-based choreography with blind and partially-sighted people in Poland (Jazdaa Polska!), making Lewisham in London the UK’s first “Borough of Literature” (London Writers Centre), and creating documentary theatre with minority groups in rural Slovakia (RAMAGU).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The latest version of Adobe Photoshop, Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0), added many AI-powered photo-editing features.
  • As The Verge reports, The New York Times sent an email to freelance photographers and contributors warning them against using Adobe Photoshop 2027.
  • The email, which was shared on social media, specifically cites features inside Photoshop that use generative AI “in ways that may not be apparent to consumers.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest version of Adobe Photoshop, Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0), added many AI-powered photo-editing features. Not all photographers are thrilled about the increasingly heavy focus on generative AI inside Photoshop, and photojournalists are taking note, too.

As The Verge reports, The New York Times sent an email to freelance photographers and contributors warning them against using Adobe Photoshop 2027.

The email, which was shared on social media, specifically cites features inside Photoshop that use generative AI “in ways that may not be apparent to consumers.”.

The Times‘ worries about Photoshop 28.0.0 are more about a perceived lack of clarity surrounding the application’s photo-editing features than the presence of AI itself. Photoshop has included generative AI in many tools for years, including Generative Remove and Generative Expand. The latest release uses generative AI for even more tasks, such as relighting and restyling photos.

Latest York Times photojournalists and freelance contributors cannot use generative AI on their photos. In fact, as the publication’s ethics standards outline, all published photos must be accurate depictions of real events. This means no people or objects can be added, rearranged, blurred, distorted, or removed. It also means that cropping must be done carefully so as not to omit any relevant details in a scene. Color can be adjusted, but only minimally and in service of accurately reproducing an event as it happened.

In a recent development, the Times adds that any use of AI, including generative AI, must be clearly disclosed to readers. The organization has long embraced Adobe’s C2PA initiative as it relates to image provenance and metadata, and that is not changing.

Industry observers note that what has changed, apparently, is how easy it is for a photographer to inadvertently use a feature inside Adobe Photoshop that relies on generative AI, which will then show up in the metadata. This appears to be the primary concern for The Newly introduced York Times, as it cannot work with photos that are labeled as AI-edited content.

According to recent reports, “It has come to our attention that certain functions in Adobe Photoshop 2027 utilize generative AI in ways that may not be apparent to users of the software. At this time we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using this new version when working on assignment for The Times,” New York Times spokesperson Graham James tells PetaPixel.

In a recent development, to prevent these issues, all contributing photographers must entirely avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignments for The Times—an unprecedented blow to Photoshop’s already wavering reputation among professional photographers. Fortunately, it is possible for users to install previous versions of Photoshop through the Creative Cloud app, although it’s not necessarily straightforward. As of this writing, users can roll back to Photoshop 27.0, but no earlier.

According to recent reports, adobe’s insistence on publicizing its generative AI features, rather than the genuinely good and mostly inoffensive improvements made earlier this month to Adobe Camera Raw and Lightroom, has created quite a stir in the photography community. The Times‘s fresh policy will certainly not help Adobe’s PR problem with photographers.

PetaPixel reached out to Adobe for comment but did not hear back ahead of publication. This story will be updated with any response.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA’s ESCAPADE spacecraft has captured an incredible photo of the Earth as it slingshotted past the planet on its way to Mars.
  • The images were taken by the spacecraft’s Visible and Infrared Observation System camera, developed by Northern Arizona University, at around 9 A.M.
  • The images were captured by the second of the two ESCAPADE spacecraft to perform a powered flyby of Earth this month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA’s ESCAPADE spacecraft has captured an incredible photo of the Earth as it slingshotted past the planet on its way to Mars.

The images were taken by the spacecraft’s Visible and Infrared Observation System camera, developed by Northern Arizona University, at around 9 A.M. EST on November 9. This was approximately three hours after the spacecraft made its closest approach to Earth, when it was about 38,500 miles away and had a clear view of the Western Hemisphere.

The images were captured by the second of the two ESCAPADE spacecraft to perform a powered flyby of Earth this month. Both spacecraft used a combination of engine burns and Earth’s gravity to gain momentum for their 10-month journey to Mars.

Once they reach orbit around the Red Planet, the spacecraft will study how the solar wind — a stream of charged particles traveling at around a million miles per hour from the Sun — interacts with Mars’ environment and contributes to the loss of its atmosphere.

A commercial satellite captured images of the pair from approximately 3,000 miles away, while a member of the mission team photographed the spacecraft passing overhead from his home near Los Angeles (below).

Two spacecraft. Two flybys. One path to Mars.

Photographed from the Los Angeles area, Blue and Gold streaked through the same part of the sky two days apart—Blue in blue, Gold in gold. https://t.co/9SDOMmqqtY.

— Rocket Lab (@RocketLab) November 23, 2026.

NASA explains that the ESCAPADE mission is funded by NASA’s Heliophysics Division and is part of the agency’s Small Innovative Missions for Planetary Exploration program. The University of California, Berkeley’s Space Sciences Laboratory leads the mission, working with partners including Rocket Lab, NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Advanced Space, and Blue Origin.

Grand Theft Auto VI takes over Miami, including its art destinations

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, a massive marketing campaign for the blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA) VI has transformed Miami—and the city’s art scene is coming along for the joyride.
  • According to recent reports, on 13 October, the street art-focused Wynwood Walls museum unveiled a collaboration with the game’s developer Rockstar Games, inviting ten artists to create GTA-themed murals in and around the museum property.
  • Industry observers note that the art-centric campaign is part of a massive marketing push around the game, which was released globally on 19 November to universal critical acclaim.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, a massive marketing campaign for the blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA) VI has transformed Miami—and the city’s art scene is coming along for the joyride.

According to recent reports, on 13 October, the street art-focused Wynwood Walls museum unveiled a collaboration with the game’s developer Rockstar Games, inviting ten artists to create GTA-themed murals in and around the museum property. The museum also declared the partnership would include merchandising and free admission for all Miami-Dade County residents until the end of 2028, reversing a pandemic-era policy that saw tickets sold at the attraction for the first time.

Industry observers note that the art-centric campaign is part of a massive marketing push around the game, which was released globally on 19 November to universal critical acclaim. Set in a satirical version of Miami called “Vice City”, the game world is an incredibly detailed virtual replica of the real city and the surrounding state of Florida (“Leonida”), complete with areas such as “Stockyard” replicating Wynwood with its street art and graffiti culture.

It has been revealed that art galleries in the digital replica of Wynwood (the "Stockyard" neighbourhood) inside Grand Theft Auto VI Screenshot by The Art Newspaper. Courtesy Rockstar Games.

Demonstrating an extreme dedication to realism, Rockstar has even painstakingly replicated and renamed local landmarks such as the nightclub Club Space (“The Vault”), the beloved regional casual dining chain Flanigan’s (“Uncle Jack’s) and local art institutions such as the Pérez Art Museum Miami ("Future Leonida Art Museum", or "Flam") and the Wolfsonian–Florida International University design museum ("Hicksonian Museum of Art and Design"). Miami Beach’s Bass Museum of Art (“Vice City Museum of Art”) had its iconic Ugo Rondinone sculpture Miami Mountain (2016) turned into a monumental stack of emojis inside the game. (Unfortunately the current exhibition at the "Vice City Museum of Art", Karl Bergstrom: Diaspora, cannot be visited as the building is not currently accessible within gameplay.).

According to Jessica Goldman Srebnick, the Wynwood Walls museum’s chief executive and curator, Rockstar commissioned in-game murals from around 50 artists, many of whom have exhibited at the museum before. When the developer approached the museum to suggest a collaboration, it was a no-brainer. “Street art and gaming have a lot of shared cultural DNA, and they’ve influenced each other,” she claims. The game’s creators “share our commitment to creativity, to supporting artists. They share our commitment and deep appreciation for the city of Miami. And I’m just really grateful that they are supporting something that provides more access to the arts.”.

A Grand Theft Auto VI-themed mural by Queen Andrea in the real Wynwood neighbourhood of Miami Courtesy Queen Andrea and Wynwood Walls Museum.

According to recent reports, the murals in Wynwood, which will be on display until 1 January 2027, are similar to those featured in the game itself. A mural by the artist Queen Andrea, for instance, reads “Welcome to Vice City” in a curvy, neon-like font, while another by Ron English features a design with grenades in the shape of lightbulbs and the slogan: “There’s nothing more dangerous than a good idea.”.

The project, as well as GTA’s larger presence in the city, has not been without controversy. The local newspaper Miami New Times reported on 10 November that one of the GTA murals had covered up a piece by the late artist Alex “Rect” Reyes, who finished the work shortly before his death in 2022. The wall had been considered a memorial by Reyes’s family and friends, who say they were not informed about its replacement. Goldman Global Arts, which owns the wall and museum, said in a statement to the New Times that it had offered Reyes’s crew a different wall to make amends.

The digital replica of Miami Beach's Bass Museum of Art within Grand Theft Auto VI, the "Vice City Museum of Art", with an emoji-themed parody of its Ugo Rondinone public sculpture Image courtesy of IGN / Official Grand Theft Auto VI Strategy Guide.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, a joint partnership with Miami-Dade County and the Miami Heat professional basketball team has resulted in everything from player uniforms to the Kaseya Center arena in Downtown Miami being rebranded with “Vice City”. Massive crowds turned out for a Heat game on 18 November, the eve of the GTA VI’s release, to purchase custom merchandise that was only available at the arena. The total package, which includes lighting and signage inspired by the game at Miami International Airport and PortMiami, is valued at $3.9m according to a press release from the county government. Some officials have expressed alarm at the collaboration, with one county commissioner worried that the game is “depicting Miami like a murder capital”, according to the Miami Herald.

As for the benefits for the local art scene, perhaps gamers who visit GTA VI’s virtual “Vice City Museum of Art” will be inspired to seek out the Bass on their next visit to Miami Beach.

Thelma Golden will step down as leader of the Studio Museum in Harlem after 21 years

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her role at the end of 2027, after a successor has been hired.
  • It has been revealed that news of Golden’s decision comes almost exactly a year after a moment of personal and institutional triumph: the opening of the Studio Museum’s new six-storey, 82,000-sq.-ft home at 144 West 125th Street.
  • Recent findings suggest that “It allows us to fully explore our ambitions, institutionally,” Golden told The Art Newspaper last year at the time of the opening.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her role at the end of 2027, after a successor has been hired. Announcing the impending leadership transition on Tuesday (24 November), Kathryn C. Chenault, the chair of the museum’s board, said Golden “is now passing on the leadership of the museum she helped build, entrusting it to a newly introduced generation she helped foster”.

It has been revealed that news of Golden’s decision comes almost exactly a year after a moment of personal and institutional triumph: the opening of the Studio Museum’s new six-storey, 82,000-sq.-ft home at 144 West 125th Street. That project had been a focus of much of the past decade of her tenure, including helping to raise a total of $322m as part of a capital campaign supporting construction and growing the museum’s endowment from $5m to $95m. The museum now has significantly more public areas; more galleries for special exhibitions and displays of its public collection; more centrally located studios for its residency programme; a rooftop terrace; and a number of key front- and back-of-house amenities it previously lacked.

Recent findings suggest that “It allows us to fully explore our ambitions, institutionally,” Golden told The Art Newspaper last year at the time of the opening. “The limitations of our two former spaces never stopped this museum from making notable, historic, significant work, it never stopped people from coming and making this a place that was important to them, it never made it so that artists didn’t want to work or engage or show here.

Industry observers note that "However, what it meant to do those things in those spaces often required incredible effort and ingenuity because they weren’t spaces made to be museums, they weren’t spaces made for art. What this space does is it not only increases our physical space, but it allows us to work in ways that we could only dream of in those former spaces.”.

The Studio Museum reopened at 144 West 125th Street in 2025 Photo: © Dror Baldinger FAIA.

It has been revealed that golden’s history at the Studio Museum spans not only her 21 years as its director, but stretches back to her years as an undergraduate student of art history and African American studies at Smith College in Northampton, Massachusetts, during which time she had an internship at the museum. After graduation, she stayed on as a curatorial fellow.

Her career then led her to the Whitney Museum of American Art, where she was initially a curatorial assistant, then the director of its off-site programme in Midtown Manhattan, and later an associate curator. During her time there she co-curated the influential 1993 Whitney Biennial (with Elisabeth Sussman) and curated Black Male: Representations of Masculinity in American Art (1994-95), a landmark examination of the construction of Black masculinity through post-war art.

Sources indicate that golden returned to the Studio Museum in 2000, when she was hired as the deputy director for exhibitions and programmes, collaborating with the then-director Lowery Stokes Sims. Golden took over the top job in 2005, when Sims stepped down. In addition to her curatorial projects—including a major Chris Ofili show in 2005 and a survey of figuration in African American Art (2002)—Golden became increasingly focused on building the Studio Museum’s future.

When preparations for demolition of its longtime home on 125th Street required the Studio Museum to close in 2018, Golden pursued partnerships with cultural and community organisations in Harlem. Building on a crucial professional development programme created with the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in 2015, she helped launch a multi-year partnership with MoMA and MoMA PS1 in 2019. This led to exhibitions of the Studio Museum’s collection and showcases for the participants in its renowned artist-in-residence programme at those institutions while construction was under way on the upcoming building.

According to recent reports, construction of the Studio Museum’s latest home was complicated by both the Covid-19 pandemic, which brought activity to a standstill, and by accusations of sexual harassment and misconduct made against its architect, David Adjaye. (He has denied all the allegations.) The site’s eventual completion and reopening, in November 2025, was seen as a triumph, creating a vastly expanded, purpose-built home for Black art that is equal to the museum’s ambitious programming and stellar permanent collection. The collection was significantly expanded during Golden’s tenure.

“I know this is the right moment to begin this transition—and as I look ahead to latest projects and opportunities, I also look back with gratitude toward the many people whose achievements have been my bedrock,” Golden said in a statement. “I think of my teachers, mentors, and professional colleagues; the long line of directors, trustees, and donors who established the Studio Museum and made it thrive; half a century’s worth of endlessly dedicated staff members, audiences and beloved Harlem neighbours; and above all the generations of artists who have enlightened us.”.

As vital to Golden’s legacy at the Studio Museum as her leadership in the building project is how her work has elevated a new generation of curators and institutional leaders, and championed artists of the African diaspora who had historically been overlooked. In her work at the Studio Museum and elsewhere, she has provided crucial support for artists including Amy Sherald, Lorna Simpson, Mark Bradford, Simone Leigh and Njideka Akunyili Crosby.

“She has nurtured the careers of countless artists; she has impacted the arc of art history; she has overseen the construction of a world-class facility in Harlem; and she has transformed the way the public thinks about art of the African diaspora,” Darren Walker, the former president of the Ford Foundation, told The Upcoming York Times. (The Ford Foundation endowed the Studio Museum's director position through a $10m grant in 2024.).

According to recent reports, in addition to her role at the Studio Museum, Golden serves on the board of directors of the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation and the Obama Foundation.

  • As Adobe Photoshop and Lightroom Product Designer, Johannes Eckert, explains on Threads, the Adobe team has worked hard to fully optimize Lightroom for Duo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, apple’s first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, has been out in the wild for a month now, and more apps are being updated to natively support the dual-screened device all the time. Adobe Lightroom just got a substantial iPhone Duo compatibility patch this week, and it is a strong example of how good the Duo can be.

As Adobe Photoshop and Lightroom Product Designer, Johannes Eckert, explains on Threads, the Adobe team has worked hard to fully optimize Lightroom for Duo.

The iPhone Duo version of Lightroom works as normal on the device’s front screen, but when opened up, it is an entirely transformed experience, showing photos much larger than on other iPhone models and moving editing tools to the side. There’s also a “laptop pose,” as Eckert says, that puts editing tools on the bottom while the photo stays above the fold.

In a recent development, in PetaPixel‘s testing, the updated app worked as promised and delivered a genuinely pleasant mobile photo editing experience. It’s nice to see my photos on the Duo’s large internal screen and to be able to access sliders, presets, masking tools, and more without obscuring my photo at all or needing to shrink it way down. You can still actually see your photo while utilizing Lightroom’s suite of editing tools, which is a major improvement over a standard iPhone photo editing experience.

That said, there is still some room for improvement, and it seems like Adobe is already working on making tweaks. For example, when doing a Curves edit, the curves themselves appear on as an overlay on the photo, which is fine, except that it leaves much of the Duo’s inner screen totally empty.

“I think it’s better to have the curves to [the] right to get rid of the empty space,” Threads user itsrongarcia commented on Eckert’s original post.

“We agree. This will be in the next enhancement!” Eckert replied.

It has been revealed that other owners are looking forward to Adobe bringing some of its more powerful editing tools over from iPad, arguing that Apple’s latest A20 Pro chip is more than capable of running things like automatic dust removal and AI-powered noise reduction. There’s no word yet on whether Adobe is considering these things at this time.

According to recent reports, adobe will no doubt refine the iPhone Duo version of Lightroom further as more real-world users get to test it out and offer their feedback, but so far, so good. Ultimately, the iPhone Duo’s lasting appeal will depend heavily on how apps utilize its distinct form factor. Lightroom is definitely taking full advantage of it, and Lightroom mobile has never been as enjoyable to use.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that never Alone 1997–2004: Raving in Europe, by Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi, features 160 original analog photographs made between 1997 and 2004.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new photography book offers a glimpse into Europe’s underground rave culture at the turn of the millennium, documenting the free-party movement through the eyes of two photographers who were part of the scene.

Industry observers note that never Alone 1997–2004: Raving in Europe, by Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi, features 160 original analog photographs made between 1997 and 2004. The images document a period when free parties were spreading across Europe, offering an alternative to mainstream society through music, community, and a shared rejection of conventional lifestyles.

Rather than documenting the movement as outsiders, Clementi and Morandi were active participants in the culture. Their photographs provide a firsthand account of a counterculture built around emotion, affection, and togetherness, at a time when music and personal connections — rather than social media and mass communication — brought people together.

According to recent reports, the book spans 196 black-and-white pages and brings together previously unseen photographs that capture the atmosphere and values of the era. Its accompanying text is written by Tobia D’Onofrio, author of Rave New World, who explores the history and significance of the European free-party movement.

“Rave was born as a disappearing ritual in which the art of invisibility was practiced, and parties were temporarily autonomous and free zones that appeared and disappeared into thin air within a few hours,” says D’Onofrio.

Recent findings suggest that “1997–2004 can therefore be considered the golden age of the so-called illegal free parties and of rave culture. It was the moment of the phenomenon’s expansion across Europe… the rave scene had been criminalized to the point that in 1994 the Criminal Justice Act in England outlawed free parties. At that point, the energies shifted to the rest of Europe, and Italy immediately became the scene of legendary parties.”.

In a recent development, the book examines how rave culture developed into more than a musical movement. It represented a rejection of conventional working and social structures, embracing communal living, constant movement, and a different relationship with time and space. Free parties became meeting places for people united by anarchic sensibilities and a desire to escape everyday routines.

Clementi and Morandi both attended the same high school in Milan before pursuing separate careers. Despite taking different paths, both remained dedicated to photography, eventually bringing their shared rave-scene experiences together in Never Alone.

The book is available online and through specialist bookstores.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A student photographer who lost his right eye after he was allegedly struck by a projectile fired by a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agent while covering a “No Kings” protest is suing the federal government.

Warning: The following photos contain content that some may find upsetting.

Industry observers note that tucker Collins, an 18-year-old freshman at the University of Southern California (USC), was left partially blind after photographing demonstrators in downtown Los Angeles on the afternoon of March 28. Collins was allegedly photographing a confrontation between protesters and federal agents when he was allegedly hit by a less-lethal projectile.

Recent findings suggest that footage indicates Collins taking pictures of demonstrators outside a federal facility before suddenly falling to his knees as a crowd-control projectile reportedly struck him in the right eye, fracturing bones in his eye socket. Collins was taken to a hospital, where he underwent two and a half hours of surgery in an attempt to save the eye. The injury was too severe, and the eye was surgically removed.

It has been revealed that collins sued the federal government on Monday, alleging that law enforcement officers used excessive force and violated his civil rights. According to a report by The New York Times, his attorneys allege that Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officers “assaulted” and “used unjustified force against him” as he photographed the protest.

The lawsuit seeks various damages from the federal government, “including past and future medical expenses, prosthetic and ophthalmologic care, educational expenses, and loss of earning capacity.”.

Industry observers note that collins’s attorney, V. James DeSimone, and his family are also demanding criminal charges against the officer responsible for shooting him. They argue that the officer’s actions violated California law governing the use of projectile launchers by law enforcement.

Sources indicate that the lawsuit also details how Collins’s injuries have limited his ability to pursue activities he once enjoyed, including photography. Collins indicates he is no longer able to safely photograph public events similar to the protest where he was injured. DeSimone also condemned the lack of criminal accountability in the wake of the shooting.

Recent findings suggest that “It is deeply disturbing that the maiming of Tucker Collins, resulting in the loss of his eye, was widely reported and captured on video and, yet, there is no law enforcement response, to date, on the Federal, State or Local level to prosecute the offending officer for his crime,” DeSimone indicates in a statement. “Once again, it is left to civil rights attorneys to attempt to achieve some semblance of justice for the permanent and irreversible harm caused to this courageous young man.”.

#114578. Mariana of Austria, royal art patron who saw power in portraiture, explored in Prado exhibition

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (729 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Mariana of Austria, royal art patron who saw power in portraiture, explored in Prado exhibition

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mariana of Austria’s position in the 17th-century Spanish court was not an easy one.
  • Sources indicate that the Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid is taking a closer look at the Spanish monarch as it opens its first exhibition devoted to a female patron of the arts.
  • “The exhibition reveals a sovereign who was not simply the subject of some of the most celebrated portraits of the Spanish Golden Age, but who understood the political power of images and actively used them to assert and legitimise her authority,” claims the exhibition curator Noelia García Pérez, a professor of art history at the Universidad de Murcia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mariana of Austria’s position in the 17th-century Spanish court was not an easy one. She became queen of Spain in 1649 after marrying Philip IV, and then when he died in 1665, she assumed the role of regent, governing for over a decade on behalf of their three-year-old son, Charles II. Her authority was challenged, repeatedly. She was also the last woman of the Habsburg dynasty to exercise governing authority within the Spanish court. Even after her regent years were over, Mariana of Austria remained a significant figurehead until her death in 1696.

Sources indicate that the Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid is taking a closer look at the Spanish monarch as it opens its first exhibition devoted to a female patron of the arts. Titled Mariana of Austria, the show reflects the museum’s efforts in recent years to re-examine historic women artists, benefactors and subjects. It includes around 100 objects, from paintings to prints and medals to manuscripts, building up a comprehensive picture of the iconography that Mariana used to curate her own public persona.

“The exhibition reveals a sovereign who was not simply the subject of some of the most celebrated portraits of the Spanish Golden Age, but who understood the political power of images and actively used them to assert and legitimise her authority,” claims the exhibition curator Noelia García Pérez, a professor of art history at the Universidad de Murcia.

Recent findings suggest that the Prado is poised to host such a presentation since it holds the most comprehensive collection of portraits of Mariana of Austria, representing every stage of her life from her youth as an Austrian archduchess up until her late years as queen mother. A full-length portrait of her by Diego Velázquez, within the Prado collection, was the model for her official image during the early years of her reign.

Frans Luycks, Infanta Mariana of Austria (around 1646)Museo Nacional del Prado.

In a recent development, mariana of Austria was in good company among other European royals who understood that authority needed a visual translation, to be communicated both domestically and across Europe. Some of the iconographic devices used by her court painters had precedents elsewhere, including among other queens. Such strategies include the use of the seated portrait, which was traditionally associated with ruling princes, and portraits in which she held a document as a reference to her governing ability.

Preparation of the exhibition has led to both a different understanding of such iconography, and a deeper knowledge of the works themselves, thanks to restorations and a reassessment of dates, identifications and attributions of several works. The exhibition also reunites rarely seen and never before exhibited works, such as a double portrait of Mariana of Austria and Charles II, on loan from the Bečov nad Teplou Castle in the Czech Republic, and a bust attributed to Nicolás de Bussy, which was recently identified as a portrait of the queen.

Another section of the exhibition is devoted to portraits of queens, regents and other female governors who held power within the Spanish monarchy over the course of roughly two centuries. “Seeing these works together reveals how attributes such as the book and the column were passed down and acquired upcoming meanings from one generation to the next,” Garcia Pérez claims, “gradually shaping a shared visual language in which piety, dynastic legitimacy and the exercise of power were closely intertwined.”.

Mariana of Austria culminates a year of focusing on three queens at the Prado—Elisabeth Farnese, Christina of Sweden and now Mariana of Austria—exploring not only their tastes but also how they used the arts as a means of asserting their authority. This focus is part of the Prado’s commitment, over the past decade, to highlight the multifaceted roles of women in art history. These initiatives have evolved into the long-term programme called The Female Perspective, which will investigate the influence of Europe’s ruling women on the arts in collaboration with the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

The next exhibition in the works will focus on female patrons of the 19th century, highlighting figures such as Spain’s Isabella II. “Ultimately, the ambition of The Female Perspective is not simply to add women’s names to an established narrative,” Garcia Pérez says. “But to enrich and, where necessary, rethink that narrative.”.

• Mariana of Austria, Museo Nacional del Prado, Madrid, until 28 March 2027.

The manifesto panel drops to a plain sans on periwinkle blue, set as one calm block of copy. The grid behind it all is the stack itself. Cards overlap like printed labels, their scalloped edges and offset corners doing the work a border would do, and the Staff Picks poster splits its wordmark top and bottom around a single bottle, dead center.

Industry observers note that the system proves itself on real surfaces.   • The mesmerizing footage indicates Earth’s natural satellite melting into the atmosphere as it disappears behind Earth.
  • “This is a real-time video of a moonset today from the space station cupola on a [Nikon] Z9 and 400mm lens,” Menon writes on his Instagram page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA astronaut Anil Menon captured a spectacular video of a moonset yesterday (Tuesday) from onboard the International Space Station.

The mesmerizing footage indicates Earth’s natural satellite melting into the atmosphere as it disappears behind Earth.

“This is a real-time video of a moonset today from the space station cupola on a [Nikon] Z9 and 400mm lens,” Menon writes on his Instagram page.

A post shared by Anil | Astronaut Space Doctor (@astro_anil).

Menon also shared a series of photos, which he specifically states contain “no edits or alterations.” Menon, a colonel in the United States Space Force, flew to the ISS in July 2026 as part of Expedition 75, for which he is a flight engineer.

A post shared by Anil | Astronaut Space Doctor (@astro_anil).

Not too long after he joined the floating space station, Menon snapped a mind-boggling photo of a super typhoon brooding above the Pacific Ocean — on his iPhone.

Just like the moonset photos, Menon took the typhoon photo from the space station’s cupola, a dome-shaped panoramic observatory module featuring six circumferential windows and a central nadir viewing window.

The cupola is where so much of the fantastic photography is made on the ISS. Menon recently shared a behind-the-scenes video showing how astronauts set up shots inside the seven-sided window.

A post shared by Anil | Astronaut Space Doctor (@astro_anil).

According to recent reports, “Welcome to the cupola,” says Menon. “This is a camera. That’s planet Earth. Here are our seven windows that we can look down at Earth with, and I’m going to take this camera and set it up for a night shot.”.

During the video, day is slowly turning to night. “Because we’re going to take a long exposure, we need to keep it stable, so we’ll set the camera up in the window, tighten it up so it’s stable, and we can put in our settings,” Menon explains.

Sources indicate that “But a lot of light is going to leak in from the sides because there’s a lot of LEDs around; there are power strips and things that can get in, so we put this shroud over the camera. That way, the lens is facing out at planet Earth, and it is hidden from the light.”.

Last week, PetaPixel highlighted German astronaut Rabea Rogge loading 35mm film into her SLR camera while in zero-gravity.

The relaunch programme includes a major show dedicated to Surrealism along with the first major retrospective for the Liverpool-based artist Chila Kumari Singh Burman. The key regional UK gallery, located on the city’s Royal Albert Dock, closed in October 2023 and was initially due to reopen in 2025.

Chila Kumari Singh Burman in front of her Winter Commission covering the façade of Tate Britain in London in 2020.

Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds, which will run until spring 2028, will include work by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray, among others. “The show will reveal the vital role of Surrealism in the history of theatre and dance, from experiments with masquerade, character and role play to major commissions for stage sets and costumes,” indicates a Tate statement. Works featured include Claude Cahun's photograph of Sheila Legge’s 1936 performance Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal, when the artist wore a Dalí-inspired costume in London's Trafalgar Square.

Claude Cahun, Sheila Legge as Surrealist ‘Phantom’, Trafalgar Square (1936).

© Claude Cahun; Image courtesy Jersey Heritage Collections.

For the overhaul, Tate Liverpool received £18.6m from the Public Bodies Infrastructure Fund, which is awarded by the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. It also received philanthropic donations from the Garfield Weston Foundation (£3m), the Wolfson Foundation (£1.25m) and the Ross Warburton Charitable Trust, alongside other trusts and individuals.

Industry observers note that the UK Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government also awarded £10m to the gallery, which it secured through a combined £20m bid with National Museums Liverpool. “We have raised more [than £30m] because there are other costs associated with reinstalling and reopening the museum,” a Tate spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper.

Sources indicate that according to a Tate statement, the designs for the new gallery, drawn up by 6a architects, “open up spaces to display the incredible variety of Tate’s collection and host world-class exhibitions. These galleries will sit alongside new public spaces for play, relaxation and learning with views across the Mersey, helping to connect the gallery with the city and the communities that surround it.” The New York and Berlin-based artist Asad Raza will create the first major commission for the gallery’s Art Hall.

Recent findings suggest that tate Liverpool, which opened in 1988, was designed by James Stirling who converted the northwest corner of a seven-story warehouse standing on the Royal Albert Dock into the five-storey gallery. It received 405,000 visitors in 2022, its last full year, and 660,000 in 2019, before the Covid-19 pandemic.

Helen Legg stepped down as Tate Liverpool director earlier this year, with Jemima Pyne taking over in the interim; a newly introduced director will be recruited after the new director of Tate, Jessica Morgan, is in post next year, the spokesperson confirmed. Tate comprises four galleries: Tate Modern, Tate Britain, Tate Liverpool and Tate St Ives.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The German government has agreed to hand over an extensive photo archive to the Jehovah’s Witnesses that documents the persecution of a pacifist Christian family under the Nazi regime.
  • Jehovah’s Witnesses were persecuted by the Nazis for their religious beliefs, particularly their refusal to serve in the military, pledge allegiance to Adolf Hitler, or participate in Nazi organizations.
  • According to a report by The Latest York Times, among those persecuted were Franz and Hilda Kusserow and their 11 children, who lived in Bad Lippspringe, a town in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The German government has agreed to hand over an extensive photo archive to the Jehovah’s Witnesses that documents the persecution of a pacifist Christian family under the Nazi regime.

Jehovah’s Witnesses were persecuted by the Nazis for their religious beliefs, particularly their refusal to serve in the military, pledge allegiance to Adolf Hitler, or participate in Nazi organizations. An estimated 4,500 Jehovah’s Witnesses were sent to concentration camps.

According to a report by The Latest York Times, among those persecuted were Franz and Hilda Kusserow and their 11 children, who lived in Bad Lippspringe, a town in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Two of the couple’s sons were executed after refusing military service because of their religious beliefs. The three youngest children were taken from their family and placed in a Nazi training school, where they were prohibited from contacting their relatives. Both parents and their remaining children were sentenced to prison terms.

Sources indicate that one of their daughters Annemarie Kusserow was arrested by the Gestapo in October 1944 and remained a prisoner until May 25, 1945, after the war in Europe had ended. Over the following decades, Annemarie gathered and preserved a collection of more than 1,000 photographs, documents, drawings, letters, and reports documenting her family’s experiences.

In her 2005 will, Annemarie bequeathed the entire photo archive to the German headquarters of the Jehovah’s Witnesses. However, her brother Hans Werner Kusserow, to whom she had loaned the collection for research purposes, sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden, Germany, in 2009. The archive has remained in the German museum’s possession ever since.

In a recent development, according to the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official website, the sale of the photo collection to a military museum was “especially troubling” given that two of Annemarie’s brothers had lost their lives because of their pacifist beliefs. The organization says the sale of the archive “resulted in years of legal battles.”.

The Jehovah’s Witnesses filed a lawsuit to recover the archive from the Bundeswehr Military History Museum, which is operated by the German armed forces. On November 19, the museum and the religious organization reached an “amicable agreement” under which the collection will be handed over to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. Both parties have agreed to keep the terms of the settlement confidential.

According to The New York Times, Sebastian Stock, a spokesman for the religious organization in Germany, states that once the transfer is complete, the “Jehovah’s Witnesses will develop and present a concept for making the archive accessible for further academic research.”.

In addition to digitizing the archive and making it available to scholars, the Jehovah’s Witnesses blueprint to display some of the documents in a new exhibition examining the history of the religious group in Central Europe.

Pixegenâs PixelLoupe is a free, open-source raw photo editor for Mac that imports Lightroom Classic catalogs without a subscription.

In a recent development, aperture disappeared years ago, and Lightroom locked photographers into monthly billing. Pixegen built PixelLoupe 1.4.3 to pick up where those tools left off, running natively on macOS 27 or later with Appleâs raw engine, Core Image, and Metal. Itâs MIT licensed, notarized by Apple, and even ships as an open Xcode project if you want to inspect the code yourself. Best of all, it keeps familiar shortcuts like G for Library, D for Develop, R to crop, and the backtick key for a 50% to 1600% pixel loupe.

On the product website, Pixegen lays out the pitch without fluff: a clean landing page leads straight to DMG and GitHub downloads, followed by side-by-side Survey comparisons and a readable feature checklist. Inside the app, the dark macOS interface feels immediately familiar. The Develop module puts your Navigator and folder tree on the left, a filmstrip along the bottom, and a draggable RGB histogram above White Balance, Tone Curve, Color Grading, and Light sliders on the right.

Industry observers note that version 1.4 brings three serious additions to this raw photo editor. First, the Remove tool lets you brush roughly over a distraction, detect the object, and fill it in with generative AI â shown clearly where the red mask over a book coverâs photo and title clears out to a plain surface. You can hit Refresh for another pass, dial back opacity, or Command-drag to sample your own source area. Second, Focus Stacking merges a run of bracketed shots, like 30 frames of a 9-volt battery, using Weighted Average, Depth Map, or Pyramid rendering with live radius and smoothing controls. Third, Assisted Culling scans a shoot for subject focus, eye focus, and open eyes before you flag keepers.

Photographers coming from Lightroom Classic 13+ can import their existing catalogs read-only, carrying over folders, collections, ratings, and develop edits while leaving original files untouched. Combined with built-in Catalog Settings for preview cache caps, duplicate detection, and automatic backups on quit, PixelLoupe gives Mac photographers full ownership of their archive again.

Brightin Star’s Gorgeous New 35mm f/1.7 APO Lens for Leica M Has Arrived

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brightin Star first unveiled its upcoming APO 35mm f/1.7 ASPH.
  • It has been revealed that the Brightin Star 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH.
  • Although rangefinder-coupled with close focusing down to 0.7 meters (2.3 feet), the lens can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet) when used in live view or adapted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brightin Star first unveiled its upcoming APO 35mm f/1.7 ASPH. lens for Leica M-Mount cameras at CP+ in February and then debuted it on Kickstarter in August. As of today, it’s available to everyone, and it’s still as handsome as ever.

It has been revealed that the Brightin Star 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. is a full-frame, manual-focus lens with a native Leica M-Mount design. However, as evidenced by the fact that Brightin Star offers it in kits with E, Z, RF, X, L, and even GFX adapters, it’s easy to adapt to other camera systems. Although Brightin Star does not state the lens’s exact image circle when used with its GFX adapter, the tech giant states it covers the 44 x 33-millimeter sensor inside GFX system medium-format mirrorless cameras.

Although rangefinder-coupled with close focusing down to 0.7 meters (2.3 feet), the lens can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet) when used in live view or adapted. Brightin Star notes that 100 degrees of focus throw covers infinity to 0.7 meters, while an additional 207 degrees covers the relatively narrow distance from 0.3 to 0.7 meters. That 307 degrees of total focus rotation is quite a lot, and Brightin Star describes it as “cinema style.”.

The 35mm f/1.7 prime is a compact, relatively lightweight lens. It measures just 43 millimeters (1.7 inches) long and weighs around 260 grams (9.2 ounces). It accepts 39mm front filters. Part of Brightin Star’s new “Apex” series of lenses, the 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. promises precision build quality and high-end optical performance.

Industry observers note that “We believe a truly exceptional M-mount lens should never have to choose between heritage and innovation,” Brightin Star notes. “The Apex Series was created with this belief at its core. It preserves the timeless, understated character of classic M lenses while bringing together advanced optics, precision mechanics, and uncompromising standards of craftsmanship.”.

Recent findings suggest that on the topic of image quality, the lens features 11 elements arranged across seven groups. There are some notable elements inside, including three double-sided aspherical lenses, three high-refractive pieces of glass, and an ED element. There are also two floating lens groups that move independently during focusing, which the manufacturer says better controls distance-related aberrations and reduces spherical aberrations at close range. The lens also promises minimized focus breathing.

As evidenced by the “APO” in its name, Brightin Star claims this is an “apochromatic” lens. While there’s no precise, industry-standard definition for what level of performance that requires, Brightin Star promises minimal chromatic aberration. An apochromatic lens focuses red, blue, and green wavelengths of light at the exact same point on the image plane. The closer a lens gets to achieving this ideal, the fewer chromatic aberrations it exhibits, all else being equal.

The Brightin Star MF 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. lens is available now for $1,099 for Leica M. An adapter adds $30, pushing the price to $1,129.

AI-Generated Characters Are Stealing Content Creators’ Viral Videos

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Content creators are increasingly discovering AI-generated versions of their videos in which almost everything is identical, except that they have been replaced by AI-generated characters.
  • From musicians and chefs to comedians, content creators are finding their performances copied by AI-generated characters that mimic their movements, jokes, and even the backgrounds in their original videos.
  • The phenomenon, known as “reskinning,” is becoming increasingly common across social media thanks to cheap and accessible AI tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Content creators are increasingly discovering AI-generated versions of their videos in which almost everything is identical, except that they have been replaced by AI-generated characters.

From musicians and chefs to comedians, content creators are finding their performances copied by AI-generated characters that mimic their movements, jokes, and even the backgrounds in their original videos.

The phenomenon, known as “reskinning,” is becoming increasingly common across social media thanks to cheap and accessible AI tools. People can take an existing video and replace the original performer with an artificial character, often designed to look funny, realistic, or hypersexualized.

The Instagram page More Perfect Union points to Higgsfield AI and its latest Genjutsu tool that allows users to upload any video file and remix it with the user’s own character, locations, or product. However, other elements of the video remain untouched.

Recent findings suggest that just a few weeks ago, Nvidia invested in Higgsfield AI in a Series B funding round that raised $400 million. It gave Higgsfield a valuation of $5.4 billion.

A post shared by More Perfect Union (@perfectunion).

Industry observers note that sophie Lloyd, a U.K.-based guitarist who tours with U.S. rapper Machine Gun Kelly, tells the BBC she has spent years building an online following, only to see AI accounts reproduce content created by musicians and other performers.

“A lot [of these accounts] are getting thousands of views, thousands of followers, just for literally doing nothing and stealing the stuff that we’ve created,” Lloyd states.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, tells the British broadcaster that the practice is often less about experimentation with AI and more about exploiting content that has already demonstrated its popularity.

“What these tools allow people to do is just automatically take a viral concept that’s already existing and to reuse it through these reskinning tools,” she says.

While some accounts may use the technology for entertainment, Kendall says others are deliberately copying successful videos in the hope of attracting an audience and generating revenue.

She sees the trend as part of a wider online “hustle culture,” in which accounts look to turn attention and engagement into money. That can mean directing followers toward subscription-based fan pages featuring adult content, promoting risky cryptocurrency products such as meme coins, or simply taking advantage of monetization features offered by social media platforms.

For the original creators, identifying and stopping the accounts responsible can be extremely difficult.

Alwyn Cruz, who has built a following on social media by exposing AI-generated musicians, describes trying to shut down these accounts as a game of whack-a-mole.

“You don’t even know who’s making these [videos]. And then if you shut it down, they’re just going to create another,” he says.

Cruz states the problem extends well beyond musicians, with performers from a variety of disciplines finding their work replicated.

“It’s not only guitarists that are being cloned: there are drummers, taekwondo players that are being cloned, and I’ve seen this all over the internet.”.

The accessibility of AI reskinning tools like Higgsfield means the practice could become increasingly difficult to contain. Creators can spend years developing an online presence and refining a style that audiences recognize, only to find that the same performances can be reproduced with a different face and a few clicks.

And while the AI-generated versions may be attracting attention, the people behind the original performances are often left watching someone else benefit from their work.

Zanele Muholi, Zanele Muholi, Tembisa, Johannesburg, 2014, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Recent findings suggest that muholi was born in 1972 in Umlazi, Durban, South Africa and lives today in Cape Town. They are a self-described visual activist, who, since the mid-2000s, have used photography to document the lives of LGBTQ+ people, initially in South Africa, where they were born.

Sources indicate that zanele Muholi, Diana Cristina Nascimento Ramos, Salvador, 2025, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

They have since expanded their project around the world and work in discrete, often ongoing series that have a common aim: to respond to violence and discrimination against queer and trans communities, to reflect their defiance and resistance, and to expand their visibility in visual culture in South Africa in particular but also far beyond.

It has been revealed that zanele Muholi, Ashara Ekundayo, Venice, 2026, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

Sources indicate that the people they depict have, since the start, been far more than sitters or subjects; they are collaborators, participants who help define the way they are represented. A crucial factor is that Muholi turns the lens onto themself. “When I position myself in my own frame,” they have said. “I do so on my own terms attempting to articulate my own way of seeing and wanting to be seen.”.

Recent findings suggest that zanele Muholi, Christine Madonsela, Daveyton, Gauteng, 2017, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

And whether it is their unflinching and tender portraits of their collaborators or their imaginative and improvised self-portraits Muholi’s photographs are always beautiful objects, with a fastidious attention to the properties and possibilities of their medium.

In a recent development, zanele Muholi, Mantedieng ‘Mantis’ Mamabolo-Cunningham, Parktown, Johannesburg, 2018, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

Industry observers note that they discuss the influence of their mother, who was a maker herself, and was a profound influence on one of their most notable works, Somnyama Ngonyama (2012). They reflect on the enormous impact of photographers including Rotimi Fani-Kayode, Lola Flash and Joan E. Biren, writers including Audre Lorde, and musicians including Brenda Fassie. A family photographer has been arrested for allegedly hiding income from her photography business to obtain more than $30,000 in food assistance benefits.

Mary Miller, a 31-year-old Wisconsin-based family photographer who operated under the name Fawn Focus Photography, is facing multiple charges related to public assistance fraud.

Industry observers note that according to a long-term investigation by the Dodge County Sheriff’s Office in Juneau, Wisconsin, Miller allegedly failed to report her earnings as a self-employed photographer while claiming FoodShare and childcare assistance benefits over several years. FoodShare is Wisconsin’s food assistance program for individuals and families with limited incomes.

According to a report by Fox 11 News, an investigation was launched after Dodge County Economic Support uncovered apparent inconsistencies between Miller’s tax records, employment records, court documents, and applications for public assistance.

Authorities allege that the photographer provided inaccurate information about her income and residency when applying for benefits, including failing to disclose earnings from her business Fawn Focus Photography.

Sources indicate that between 2019 and 2025, Miller allegedly received more than $30,000 in FoodShare benefits that she was not entitled to claim. She also received more than $22,000 in childcare assistance benefits, although investigators were still determining how much of that funding was improperly obtained.

Recent findings suggest that according to online court records, Miller faces six counts of failing to disclose an event affecting her eligibility for benefits and six counts of failing to report the receipt of income or assets. The photographer made her initial court appearance this month and was issued a $5,000 signature bond.

According to recent reports, “Public assistance programs exist to help individuals and families during times of genuine need and are funded by hardworking taxpayers,” Dodge County Sheriff Dale J. Schmidt tells Fox 11 News in a statement. “When someone is alleged to have concealed income or provided false information in order to obtain benefits, it undermines public trust and diverts limited resources away from those who legitimately qualify for assistance.”.

According to recent reports, previously, PetaPixel reported on a photographer who was sentenced to five years in federal prison for defrauding a family out of $4.6 million and using $200,000 of the money to purchase Taylor Swift concert tickets. 46-year-old photographer Chanise Coyne was given jail time after pleading guilty to wire fraud over a multimillion-dollar fraud scheme involving fictional child modeling events.
